This study investigates a grounded state $u$ of the Schrödinger operator $-u''$ on $[0,1]$ with a potential function $Q\in L^0$ as its leading coefficient. We demonstrate that when the weighted Barron space $\mathcal{B}^{(1)}(Q)$ contains solely polynomials, the grounded state $u$ can be approximated uniformly to any degree of accuracy. Furthermore, if the weighted Barron space $\mathcal{B}^{(2)}(Q)$ contains all polynomials of degree less than or equal to $k$, a unique grounded state $u_k$ emerges, which converges to $u$ at the rate of $|u_k(u)|_{L^\infty}$ to the order $O(1/n^k)$. Last but not least, when $Q\in L^0$ is constant everywhere, our findings reveal that $u$ lies within the spectral Barron space $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{S}(H_Q))$, which further implies that $u$ can be approximated uniformly to any degree of accuracy. Using a modified version of the Haastad usefulness inequality along with the spectral handshaking theorem, our results can provide novel bounds for the least $l_1$-norm Steiner cut problem and weighted Boolean satisfiability problem. Interestingly, our study reveals that when $Q\equiv 1$, the grounded state $u$ lies within the unweighted Barron space $\mathcal{B}^{(2)}(1)$, which also contains all polynomials of degree less than or equal to $k$, a discovery demonstrating the substantial similarity between weighted and unweighted grounded states. Ultimately, our investigations shed light on novel connections between weighted variational problems and weighted Barron spaces. Specifically, our study reveals that when $Q\equiv 1$, the weighted least action solution $u$ can be approximated uniformly to any degree of accuracy to the order $O(1/n^k)$, a finding which also applies to similar problems. Moreover, our results can provide novel bounds for related problems like the unweighted least action solution of the Schrödinger equation and the unweighted Boolean satisfiability problem, both of which can be achieved at the rate of $O(1/n^k)$. The intricacy of the human nervous system makes studying simpler organisms, such as C. Elegans, valuable for gaining insights into brain activity. With well-documented behavioural and structural biology, C. Elegans serves as a suitable model for testing simulation techniques and modelling approaches. Traditional white-box models that rely on internal details of these neural networks are inadequate for capturing the complex responses to stimuli or lead to overly complicated simulations. In this research, we use data-driven methods with advanced recurrent neural networks, such as LSTMs and GRUs, to simulate C. Elegans' nervous system and compare the models in terms of performance, simplicity, and reliability. Notably, GRU models with 4 hidden units exhibit high precision in replicating the organism's varied responses to stimuli. To compare model effectiveness, we introduce a new benchmark that considers not only dynamic responses but also the organisation and structure of the neural system. Moreover, we propose an approach for integrating electrophysiological data and behavioural information to improve the accuracy of simulated responses. Lastly, we explore the possibilities of extrapolating simulated data from C. Elegans to other organisms, such as D. Melanogaster. The work mentioned above can be found at https://github.com/brain-machine/c_elegans_gru. A novel, straightforward sorting method is applied to permutations: repeatedly insert the permutation's initial element into the corresponding position, stopping once it becomes 1. This process yields a distinct structural pattern involving the set of all permutations, with permutations beginning with 1 at the top and those without fixed points, known as derangements, at the bottom. Observing this pattern from a different perspective and tracing it from top to bottom leads to a similar process where one selects a fixed point and shifts it to the start. It has been proven that the number of steps in this process for a given size n follows a Poisson distribution with the same mean and variance, further characterizing the long-term behavior. Furthermore, similar findings apply to cycles of permutations with a specific number of elements. In contrast, a contrasting pattern arises when following the paths from the bottom up, and by using the generating function method, it can be shown that the number of steps in this path also follows a Poisson distribution with the same mean and variance. Building upon this, further studies are conducted on permutations with a specific number of elements or a specific number of cycles. In addition to these findings, a different structural pattern is discovered for permutations with a specific number of elements or a specific number of cycles. By using either the first element-based approach or the fixed point-based approach, it can be shown that the shortest path to the bottom follows a geometric distribution with the same mean. Finally, these findings lay the groundwork for a unique and intricate "sorting landscape," in which the "height" is defined as the number of fixed points and the "width" is the number of cycles. Interestingly, the first element-based approach results in a landscape with distinct layers separated by straight lines, while the fixed point-based approach creates a landscape with curved layers, both leading to similar patterns of permutation graphs. However, the novel, geometric-distribution-based method reveals significantly distinct behaviors, with both methods displaying and rejecting previous theories of linear relationship between the height and width. Instead, a distinct, nonlinear pattern emerges when taking the base-10 logarithm of the width with respect to the height. In a set of permutations known as "cyclic" permutations, a perfect linear relationship is observed. By generalizing the concept of "smoothing" from the works of Diaconis and Worsley to the entire set of permutations, a perfect linear relationship is obtained when considering all possible values of the height. Results show that the $\sigma$ and $\kappa$ pentquark states can be entirely composed of $udddd$ quarks or $\epsilon$ quarks, respectively, or a combination of $udd$ quarks and irreducible diquark $\bar{d}u$. Notably, the study finds that the diquark leads to a non-zero charge radius for the $\kappa$ state, unlike the sigma. Further examination of the issue could lead to a more thorough understanding of the structure of pentaquark particles. It is suggested that the quark-diquark P-wave pentaquark states, though not examined here, may provide another means of investigating the same concept. Investigating orbital resonances enables the restriction of planetary properties in compact systems. The early K-type star K2-138, hosting five planets, particularly five proposed resonant planets (d through h) with different simulated configurations, has raised questions about its planetary arrangement. To address this, our study used a comprehensive approach leveraging various techniques to examine possible resonant configurations in system simulations, taking into consideration established astrophysical constraints. Results from detailed dynamical simulations of all possible resonant scenarios indicated that a chain of 3:2 resonances among the planets is highly likely, accounting for approximately 95% of simulations, whereas successive resonances did not persist through long-term dynamical simulations. Notably, combining orbital resonances and constraints on the planetary sizes and distances yielded a relatively narrow range for each planet's mass: between approximately 0.276 to 0.430 M_R, with d being the heaviest at 0.356 M_R, whereas e, f, and g had decreasing masses, and c, in the resonant scenario, was closest to 0.23 M_R. Further examination of this system demonstrated that its projected orientation and 242-day orbit period of the star make it an unsuitable candidate for the OPPS (Optically Pulsating Pulsar Systems) project. Nonetheless, its uniqueness as a compact planetary system makes it an important discovery in astrophysical understanding. Additionally, its stability in long-term dynamical simulations has revealed its potential as a reference point for comparable systems in studies of planetary stability. Lastly, its observed transit depths, coupled with astrophysical constraints on the masses and orbit distances, have further pinpointed the possible masses for each planet in the resonant scenario. These findings highlight the significant contributions possible resonant configurations make to our comprehension of compact planetary systems like K2-138. Finally, its long-term orbital stability in simulated scenarios has potential implications for future space missions, seeking similar systems, and in the design of missions themselves, such as those aiming to detect, extract, and analyze signals generated by planetary systems in various stages of formation. At least one exoplanet in such systems could yield significant mass in potential space missions, influencing spacecraft dynamics and the information extracted from signals of the various planets, whereas active manipulation of the spacecraft position could enhance our understanding of the planetary properties by extending the operational life of the spacecraft. At least one exoplanet in targeted systems could yield substantial mass in potential space missions, modulating spacecraft dynamics and information extracted from signals of the various planets

When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An innovative measure, based on the arrangement of oxygen atoms in the ice structure, allowed the researchers to confirm that LDA and HDA do not contain separate ice domains but are instead homogeneous samples of the same phase. Similarly, when the pressure is released, both LDA and HDA transform into Ih ice, showing that the transitions are not influenced by the type of ice phase. However, when the pressure is slowly increased on LDA, it smoothly transforms into HDA, while rapidly increasing the pressure results in the direct transformation of Ih ice into HDA, eliminating the possibility of an intermediate transition into LDA. These observations provide significant insights into the mysterious properties of LDA and HDA, while revealing that the transition between them is a gradual process that does not involve distinct phases. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've analyzed their physical properties by applying a method that uses the counterterm, which was inspired by AdS/CFT correspondence. This has allowed us to calculate mass and angular momentum, and we have determined both the thermal stability and scalar field behavior. The underlying text representation schemes, crucial to these advancements, have a significant impact on the overall performance of the system. The SSR framework incorporates multiple components, including building semantic associations, encoding complex information with recall constraints, introducing recall influences, and developing efficient computing models. The theoretical foundations of SSR, including its applications and improvements, have been rigorously explored. The findings demonstrate SSR's efficacy in processing semi-formal and formal text with improved accuracy and efficiency, across various NLP tasks. The empirical studies show SSR's ability to outperform established text representation schemes while efficiently handling English and Chinese text datasets. The results suggest SSR's vast potential in enhancing text mining and processing systems. The database is enriched with numerous datasets from prominent NLP projects, all incorporated into the SSR framework. The incorporation of human knowledge and machine learning in the SSR framework has the potential to significantly boost the performance of general and deep learning systems, even those processing large amounts of text, by tapping into the vast knowledge and efficiency of the SSR scheme. The inclusion of the SSR framework and its accompanying database offers an opportunity for researchers to collaborate and contribute to the development of more advanced text representation and processing systems. A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly reflecting how programs operate, whereas corresponding big-step semantics describe a calculation as an uninterrupted process culminating in a final value.  A convenient method exists for transforming small-step to big-step semantics but it sometimes distorts the original semantics. In certain cases, these transformations lead to enhanced operational density where a single judgment statement can validate an entire judgment family.
We have discovered that this convenient method is not a reliable general tool. In a 2009 paper in top conference POPL, we presented a new method that guarantees the faithful translation of small-step to big-step semantics. The approach leverages multi-stage types and simplifies the process by capitalizing on the assumption that operational density does not increase during the translation process.
In this paper, we demonstrate that the assumption of operational density preservation is too stringent and derive a more practical notion that can serve as an alternative. We further introduce a type system that enforces this new guarantee and provide mechanisms to ensure that the assumption holds for existing languages with small-step semantics. As a result, this solution provides a reliable way to transfer the semantics of a programming language from a small-step to a big-step framework. We have applied this solution to several significant programming languages including PCF, NP, STk, λst, and uncurry. An interesting aspect of our method is that, unlike typical operations with increased density, our solutions preserve the original structure of these languages even when they involve recursive functions. As such, our method offers an appealing way to simplify the semantics of programming languages that have been altered to incorporate new syntactic forms. In general, our technique can be used to develop new logical judgments about the behavior of programming languages that operate according to small-step operational semantics. This research introduces a sophisticated classifier capable of identifying both operational and non-operational internal faults in Indirect Symmetrical Phase Angle Regulating Transformers through analysis of electrical disturbance signals. The proposed classifier, grounded in a convolutional neural network structure, possesses flexibility and adaptability, allowing it to distinguish between various types of faults without requiring in-depth technical knowledge. By evaluating numerous samples under diverse conditions, the study showcases the efficacy of the proposed classifier in accurately identifying several types of faults, including those caused by mechanical and electrical issues, as well as transient phenomena. The proposed approach encompasses real-time feature extraction using instantaneous symmetrical components of the fault signals, thereby optimizing computational efficiency and achieving start-up and rise-to-maturity fault classification within 50 milliseconds. Moreover, the fault detection model is tailored to address generalization challenges by incorporating augmented data generated through random transformations into the training dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed classifier outperforms existing conventional fault diagnosis methods in several key performance metrics, including fault discrimination accuracy, false fault rates, and fault detection rates. To further disseminate the classifier's capabilities, a user-friendly web interface has been developed to facilitate user-generated fault classification for previously unseen data. The proposed classifier, along with its associated documentation and web interface, is publicly available for further research and development purposes. Moreover, the classification results can be employed to estimate the fault locations, instantaneously, utilizing the developed approach. The proposed classifier's documentation comprises detailed specifications, including the implementation of the CNN algorithm using Python code, the dataset compilation process, and the design of the web interface utilizing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, all rendered through an HTML template. By integrating the classifier into an intelligent monitoring system, the classification results can be utilized as an estimate of the fault location, demonstrating the potential of the proposed approach in enhancing the reliability of the power system. The proposed classification results demonstrate a significant enhancement of the fault detection and discrimination capabilities when compared to existing conventional methods, achieving a fault detection rate of approximately 85.71% for mechanical faults, 94.31% for electrical transient faults, and 98.22% for non-fault electrical disturbance signals. A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined by two growth patterns: one growing and the other shrinking, both following the form 2 raised to a power of n times a constant greater than 0. In this paper, techniques are developed to detect the near-exponential nature of certain sums that arise from sums of geometric series and inner sums. Specifically, near-exponential growth is proven in the sums of unique combinations of n elements from sets with a finite number of elements, and in the sums of unique pairs from sets with a finite number of elements. These findings have an additional constraint that no element can appear in more than one pair. Similar results are also derived for the sums of unique non-negative integer sequences. Near-exponential bounds are established for the rates of convergence of several infinite series, including the binomial and Stirling series, when truncated to a finite number of terms. An in-depth analysis of the Kolmogorov-Lummer-Stirling type inequalities also reveals near-exponential bounds for the rates of convergence. This research implies a near-exponential upper limit to the length of shortest schemes that can encode all n-element combinations exactly. Specifically, we derive near-exponential bounds for the rates of n-element combinations encoding schemes, and show that this is nearly optimal by proving that some cases require lengths that grow exponentially. Furthermore, near-exponential bounds are derived for the rates of n-element combinations encoding schemes with the additional constraint that pairs cannot share elements. This research has an additional application in discovering new Coppersmith Coppersmith-Sudler type inequalities. Specifically, we discover near-exponential bounds for the rates of n-element combinations encoding schemes with the additional convenience of encoding pairs simultaneously. This research has an additional application in discovering a near-exponential bound for the rates of membership testing that uses AEB data structures. Specifically, we discover that for a finite abelian group, there is a near-exponential bound for the rates of membership testing that uses optimal schemes, and shows that some cases require lengths that grow exponentially. This research implies a near-exponential bound for the rates of AEB data structures in the context of polynomial codes. Specifically, we discover that for a finite abelian group, there is a near-exponential bound for the rates of AEB data structures in the optimal scheme, and since this is known to be one of the most efficient schemes possible, it is nearly optimal. Superconducting qubit performance is constrained by dielectric loss. Experimental evidence sets upper limits on dielectric loss tangents, approximately $100$ parts-per-billion, however the dielectric loss mechanism remains unclear. Specifically, it has not been determined whether dielectric loss is caused by bulk dielectric properties, surface impurities, or ionic contamination. We employ a precision dielectric measurement technique to investigate bulk dielectric loss in a cryogenic situation for the first time. This method involves using an 'on-substrate' SiN microdisk resonator with an embedded dielectric nanofoil to measure dielectric properties. Our study shows that SiN microdisk resonators can detect dielectric loss tangents as low as $10$ parts-per-billion with accuracy. Furthermore, we confirm that bulk dielectric loss is the primary cause for tangents within this range. This is characterized via ion release from substrate by means of radio-frequency spin-resonance, verifying that bulk dielectric loss far exceeds loss to surface impurities. This study lays the groundwork for future improvements to superconducting qubits, enabling performance limits to be pushed lower. Dielectric nanofoil technology may also enable analysis of various materials for their dielectric properties at multiple frequencies. Moreover, as dielectric nanofoils have extremely low bulk volumes, this technique can detect very minor contamination within ultra-pure dielectric materials. This study may also contribute to ongoing discussions regarding dielectric nanofoil applications in quantum technology. With advancements in low-loss dielectric materials, our technique may detect tangents as low as $1$ parts-per-billion in the future. This is particularly important as the dielectric nanofoil technique may soon detect contamination which is currently undetectable, e.g. for high-purity oxide dielectric materials. Conversely, if surface loss were a major factor, tangents exceeding $10^5$ would be measured, indicating that surface loss could be reduced to superconducting qubit performance limits. Alternatively, this study demonstrates that bulk dielectric performance improvements could enable performance limits to be pushed lower; e.g. reducing SiN loss tangents from $10^3$ to $10^4$ would increase qubit coherence times by one order of magnitude. A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a novel optical drag effect where the path deviation is positively correlated with the square of the medium's velocity. The phenomenon arises specifically in scenarios where the medium under observation is comprised of a waveguide system subjected to acceleration, and to observe this effect, we must also ensure the light source is positioned outside the system. Our findings demonstrate that the path deviation can be quantified based on the optical drag constant, where this constant is directly linked to the accumulated phase shift incurred by the light as it travels through the system. To verify the existence of this effect, we suggest conducting an experiment involving a monochromatic light source, a moving waveguide system, and measuring the induced path deviation. Possible applications of this new optical drag effect could involve employing it as an atomic sensitivity metric to identify subtle changes in accelerating massive objects, thus providing a means to test the equivalence principle at a microscopic scale compatible with optical techniques. Moreover, this effect could also contribute to advancements in optical metrology by enabling the measurement of accelerations smaller than the currently attainable value with today's technology. Lastly, our study reveals that the new optical drag effect remains unaffected by the specific characteristics of the light used in the experiment, whether coherent or incoherent. The distinct behavior of the optical drag effect under accelerating conditions, in comparison to the established optical drag effect that varies linearly with velocity and has a sensitivity $n$, could enable the creation of a specific mixture of both effects by using a system composed of multiple waveguides. This would allow for a detailed analysis of the optical drag effect, and our theoretical model can predict whether an optical drag constant is positive, negative, or zero, depending on certain parameters. To further explore this topic, we have developed a detailed framework for examining optical drag effects in waveguide systems and developed a method to observe and identify both the linear and the quadratic optical drag effect, and show that the quadratic effect, although appearing similar to the linear effect, has distinct characteristics. Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to lack of structure in the resulting linear system and partly due to inefficient use of available information about parameter preferences. We overcome these challenges by developing three exact calculation methods that leverage structural information about the resulting linear system and incorporate preferred value information in an efficient manner. These methods result in equivalent descriptions of counterexample parameters as linear systems of equations and provide a new approach to solving robust optimization problems in two stages. We note that existing methods for calculating worst-case scenario parameter realization often fail to identify preferred counterexample parameters when they exist, and we propose a new post-optimality analysis method that identifies all parameter realizations with optimal objective functions. This method is generally applicable to various forms of robust optimization problems and can be implemented using existing linear programming software. We provide numerical results showing that our new methods outperform existing alternatives in terms of runtime and significantly reduce computational effort in many cases. We leverage the structure of the resulting linear system, incorporating an algorithm for calculating nullspace bases based on the adjoint matrix, which is currently unavailable in standard software. We propose a new implementation of this calculation method that has currently negligible computational cost in practical examples and is based on the representation of a vector space as the nullspace of a matrix. This idea is generally applicable to various fields and can be efficiently implemented in various settings. We provide numerical results showing its effectiveness in linear programming, convex quadratic optimization, and linear systems of equations. We also extend it to efficiently solve binary linear systems of equations and present a new calculation method for calculating worst-case parameter realization in two-stage robust optimization problems involving uncertain continuous data. Deep learning models' success in graph spaces is largely attributed to the development of graph neural networks (GNNs). Like their conventional counterparts, GNNs benefit from transfer learning by leveraging pre-trained components to expedite learning in new, unrelated tasks. Contemporary approaches lack the capacity to adapt GNNs to new tasks effectively as they were originally designed for supervision within the same graph. Moreover, existing methods in transfer learning do not account for the unique structure adaptations required by GNNs. To address these concerns, we introduce a novel strategy, Backward Transfer Learning (BTL), aimed at transferring knowledge from a source to a target graph without explicit supervision. BTL utilizes a two-stage process: Initially, it develops an orthogonal projection layer ('2B') to extract features from the source graph, which it then applies backwards to capture similarities in the target graph. This innovative scheme necessitates an orthogonal projection to ensure consistency and maintain the structure of the learned representation. Moreover, it develops an objective function based on the constraint of the orthogonality of the projection layer, along with a new loss function for metric learning that utilizes the distance between the source and target graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that BTL's application accelerates GNN training and leads to better outcomes in various scenarios across three benchmark datasets. Additionally, case studies focusing on task evolution, domain adaptation, and inductive learning confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself when low-temperature 2D harmonic oscillator traps hold fermions at the ground state. As a result, the lack of interaction between fermions leads to the formation of Pauli crystals. This occurrence can be observed in the experiment by Roos et al. for $^{40}$K, and for the first time, the exclusion principle has been demonstrated in the case of the middle energy level in a harmonic oscillator trap. The measured exclusion principle splitting (EPS) corresponds precisely with the quantum theoretical prediction. This study aims to re-examine the suitability and adaptability of Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN) for solving various real-time differential and integral equation problems, as well as multi-objective optimization issues. ZNN has emerged as a popular method for these problems, and recent research has highlighted its potential for handling multi-objective optimization problems, although there is a lack of definitive proof comparing its suitability with that of implicit dynamical systems. Therefore, this study seeks to introduce a novel approach based on implicit dynamical systems to tackle multi-objective optimization problems, and compares its implications with those of ZNN. We propose a new multi-objective optimization technique, with a dynamic analytical error that decreases over time, and we prove that this error decreases exponentially. Furthermore, this method exhibits comparable precision to that of ZNN, although our approach allows for more flexible selection of hyperparameters. We also observe that multi-objective optimization problems can be categorized into different types, and we propose an algorithm that calculates the corresponding characteristic multi-objective configuration function using the Jacobian matrix of the system. This function determines the eligibility of a particular point on the Pareto front, and enables the development of an optimization algorithm that ensures asymptotic convergence to the Pareto front. We test the efficacy of our approach on multi-objective optimization problems under different settings, and compare the results with those of the ZNN method. Our results demonstrate that the Pareto front points calculated by both methods converge exponentially, and the proposed method enables the selection of specific Riemannian manifold hyperparameters, such as the dimension of the tangent space, to facilitate convergence. Notably, our approach allows for faster convergence than ZNN, and our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our technique for both small and large multi-objective optimization problems. Finally, we highlight potential areas for further investigation regarding multi-objective optimization problems, and suggest integrating learning-based techniques to improve the efficiency and suitability of the proposed method. In particular, this study proposes a learning-based approach to finding the optimal multi-objective configuration function, and evaluates its efficacy using several optimization algorithms. Our results show that the learned functions of the proposed method enable faster convergence than ZNN, and our approach enables the simulation of different scenario models using the calculated configuration functions. Our experiments also demonstrate the suitability of our approach for solving multi-objective optimization problems in various fields, and our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed learning-based technique for real-world problem solving. In addition, this study proposes an alternative approach called Multi-objective Dynamic Analytical Error Implicit Dynamical Systems

Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment as crucial tools for determining the most cost-effective and feasible generation schedules. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be conservative and leaves a considerable percentage of constraints intact. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a machine learning-based model to predict costs given load inputs, enabling more effective optimization and constraint screening in unit commitment problems. By incorporating cost perspectives and machine learning, the proposed model outperforms conventional approaches, significantly reducing computational time across various scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our model in predicting unit commitment costs under uncertain line outages. To achieve this, we first estimate probabilistic line outage rates based on actual system data, employing statistical methods to analyze a dataset of 365 days. By employing this estimated data as input, our machine learning-based model generates cost predictions, thereby facilitating more accurate robust optimization solutions with substantially decreased computational time. Detailed evaluation of our model's performance involves numerical simulations using actual system data, showcasing its capability to predict costs, identify non-screened constraints, and accurately quantify complementary uncertainty risks. Moreover, our model's screening accuracy far exceeds that of conventional methods, reducing feasible sets by up to 94% in some cases. With its impressive ability to anticipate costs and mitigate constraints, our model has the potential to vastly expedite the solution process for transmission-constrained unit commitment problems on large-scale power systems. Furthermore, our model's design is adaptable and can easily be applied to other power system optimization problems. To facilitate this, we provide publicly accessible pre-trained models that can achieve a substantial decrease in computational time, thereby beeing highly valuable for transmission system operators. Ultimately, our machine learning-based model offers a pioneering solution to accurately forecast costs, minimize computational time, and minimize system operator workload. It has been discovered, however, that traditional estimation techniques can be inconsistent. Determining similarity between structured data, especially graph structures, is a fundamental problem that has been crucial in multiple applications of data mining and machine learning. Recent advances in Gromov-Wasserstein distance have highlighted its potential to effectively capture topological and feature-based similarities while also addressing issues related to data permutations. Nevertheless, structured data are widely dispersed across different organizations and can only be accessed on a limited scale due to concerns about privacy. To resolve this dilemma, a privacy-protecting framework is presented that analyzes, in a distributed fashion, the discrepancies in Gromov-Wasserstein distances from multiple data sources without necessitating the sharing of the entire data sets. Furthermore, this framework incorporates a novel denoising technique that utilizes network architecture to minimize the effects of noise in the estimated distances. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that it surpasses existing methods both in terms of node classification and graph-level link prediction. To ensure the privacy of sensitive information, a theoretical analysis of the privacy risks is conducted and a novel optimization method is developed to minimize these risks while maintaining accurate estimations of the Gromov-Wasserstein distance. The experiments demonstrate that it is feasible to attain a balance between robustness and estimations by limiting the precision of node labels and the graph connections. The dynamics of background electron injection into a developing plasma bubble behind an extremely powerful laser beam is a multifaceted phenomenon influenced by two primary mechanisms. As an intense laser beam traverses a plasma, forming a shock-like steepened edge, these mechanisms act in tandem. Meanwhile, periodic plasma bubble oscillations along the laser beam path can either hinder or cooperate with electron injection driven by bubble expansion. Research has shown that CEP-managed plasma bubble oscillations generated by the laser beam's self-modulation can create an unique electron injector: the EPUB, or Expanding Phase controlled Undulating Bubble. By regulating the EPUB with laser polarization and power, scientists have been able to produce extremely charged (multiple nanocoulombs) high-current (tens of kiloamperes) electron beams with very short (femtosecond scale) temporal structures, observed directly in experiment aftertons. Moreover, these beams can create a highly confined high-density plasma with potential applications for radiation generation, acceleration, and confinement. Notably, the potential of the EPUB-based injector lies not only in fundamental research but also in a diverse array of applications and technologies. This study presents a comprehensive model explaining how and why EPUB is formed, the factors influencing its development, and their interrelations, offering guidance for optimizing and leveraging this novel electron injector for a wide range of research and industrial applications. Further, it outlines prospects for expanding on an extensive range of light-matter interactions. This work lays a foundational path for investigating light-matter interactions. A platinum foil with a mass of 45.3 grams was measured over a period of 510 days at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy to study its low-level radioactivity and serve as a high voltage contact within a detector made from a high purity germanium crystal. The collected data allowed for an in-depth examination of various decay modes exhibited by naturally occurring isotopes of platinum, specifically focusing on double beta decay into excited states and other possible modes. The results revealed limits of double beta decay ranging from $10^{14}$ to $10^{17}$ annual rates (at a 90% confidence level) and also set new standards in this area while confirming and extending previously discovered limitations. In addition to these findings, the investigation provided current upper bounds on electron capture followed by positron emission and double electron capture in platinum-192 isotopes with limits of $1.0\times 10^{11}$ annual rates (at a 90% confidence level) and also provided a new restriction on this process in platinum-194 with a limit of $0.58\times 10^{11}$ annual rates (at a 90% confidence level). Finally, the observed limits of this decay method in platinum-192 and platinum-194 isotopes are among the most stringent recorded to date. The presented data will serve as a reference point for interpreting future experiments focusing on these particular decay methods. Furthermore, we discuss the possibilities of utilizing detectors based on semiconductors to study rare nuclear processes in various platinum isotopes in the future. Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic crystal fibers, showcasing a substantial conversion efficiency between the HE11 and HE21 modes and reaching a peak gain coefficient of 21.4/W/km. By investigating mechanical resonances with various symmetries, we identify both mode-dependent and mode-independent interactions in intermodal Brillouin effects, which are crucial factors to consider in engineering the structures of photonic crystal fibers to boost high-order optical mode coupling through flexural mechanical resonances, as influenced by factors like squeeze film air damping and leakage. Through numerical simulations based on a combined optical-mechanical modeling approach, we gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms, revealing that anti-symmetric mechanical resonances can provide a more efficient aero-statically stable structure for intermodal coupling, which may have significant implications for various applications such as Brillouin fiber gratings, optical cavities, and sensing platforms, and further, serving as the foundation for developing novel photonic bandgap-based optical resonators. As a final note, the theoretical framework laid out in this study can also be applied to related studies on optical parametric amplifications via anti- Stokes processes in solid-core photonic crystal fibers. 

Keywords: Brillouin scattering, photonic crystal fibers, optical measurements, mechanical resonances, coupled optical-mechanical systems.

Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items from a set to minimize cost while maximizing the value of the included elements, with the key difference being that the first allows for repeated selections while the second does not. However, each has its own set of objectives. Surprisingly, there is no single algorithm known to solve both, leading us to design and test a novel dynamic programming solution that successfully addresses both variants efficiently, despite being initially proposed for the SUKP. Our extensive analysis reveals SUKP algorithms outperformed traditional dynamic programming for the BMCP, with our new approach even offering improved performance over existing state-of-the-art solutions for the SUKP and notable gains over a previously best-known BMCP algorithm. In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the Fock term leads to the creation of a photon potential that varies with energy. This results in the photon-photon interaction having a characteristic that is similar to that of the photon form factor, which in turn gives rise to the tri-photonic process $\gamma + \gamma \to \gamma + \gamma$. A calculation was subsequently conducted to determine the cross-section of this new process. Interestingly, it was discovered that the cross-section of this process is almost entirely independent of the photon's energy, meaning that it generates a fixed effective cross-section. As a consequence, the tri-photonic process offers the potential to study photon-photon interactions in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions across a broad range of photon energies. Furthermore, combining this process with photon-jet and photon-photon interactions may enable researchers to differentiate between their individual contributions more effectively. A study was also conducted to assess the tri-photonic process's influence on the photon-jet phenomenon and researchers discovered that, at a specific energy of 200 GeV, this process contributes around 4% of the photon-jet's cross-section. An in-depth examination of the tri-photonic process's characteristics was also undertaken in order to facilitate its distinction from other photon-jet and photon-photon interaction phenomena. It was also proposed that future research at the FCC-hh photon-photon collider may be able to utilize the tri-photonic process to investigate quantum effects such as BRS non-consistencies, hinting towards new physics beyond the Standard Model. A final proposal was put forth, suggesting that an in-depth study of quantum effects on tri-photonic process would be essential for constructing a quantum-corrected Glauber model that could accurately account for photon-jet and photon-photon interactions.

To minimize pollution, bicycle usage is experiencing a resurgence, particularly in urban environments. Despite the trend towards sustainable transportation, cyclists remain at a higher risk of accidents. The existing assessment methods, typically used by transportation authorities, have significant drawbacks, including a focus on numerical data and a decision-making process heavily influenced by human judgment. This approach can be costly, time-consuming, and potentially biased, resulting in lengthy assessment processes. In contrast, we introduce an image-based framework that evaluates road conditions from a safety perspective. Our framework relies on artificial intelligence to gather relevant information from visual data, eliminating the need for manual collection of data regarding accidents. In addition to reducing traffic-related accidents, this technology has the potential to expand to other safety aspects, such as air quality monitoring. To develop our framework, we designed a novel model called CycleRisk, which takes an aerial map as input and generates text descriptions or visual attention maps to inform authorities. CycleRisk significantly outperforms existing models in this field, as verified in experiments using the public RoadNoise, CycleVision, and TrafficCam datasets. In particular, our framework achieves impressive performance on the CycleVision dataset, processing images at a speed of 11.7 frames per second, while accurately predicting cycle risks based on visual data while ignoring irrelevant objects. This breakthrough enables authorities to quickly assess and monitor cycling route safety more efficiently. Furthermore, CycleRisk's capabilities can be utilized to explain decision-making processes through its attention maps. These maps provide valuable insights into the importance of specific road features to users. To support the community, we have made CycleRisk publicly available under an open-source license. Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, these networks lose their capacity for constraint and consequently remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Similar reasoning can be applied to other deep neural networks featuring set operations that yield identity mappings. It's also worth noting that neural networks combining with convolutional and recurrent layers, including those using orthogonal initialization, have similar theoretical constraints limiting their ability to contain malicious interference. In contrast, a neural-ODE model, introduced in this paper, enjoys inherent robustness against malicious interference, achieving this through the integration of an adaptive gradient descent scheme, which facilitates a reduction in gradient norms resulting from adversarial inputs. This robustness, along with the model's capacity for intrinsic generalizability, makes it an attractive choice. Experiments conducted on popular datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny-ImageNet as well as the well-known CIFAR-10 adversarial dataset confirm the effectiveness of the model. When compared to other countermeasures including Jacobian regularization, adversarial training, batch renormalization, layer-wise adversarial training, and Adversarial Disc, our model exhibits superior performance. Our model's source code is available at: https://github.com/azazzaa/azazzaa/tree/main/RO-NOde. In terms of theoretical contributions, this paper addresses a fundamental question regarding inherent robustness in deep neural networks, including those using orthogonal initialization. Additionally, this paper proposes essential requirements for achieving inherent robustness based on the model's specific design. These conditions are applicable to neural networks featuring set operations that yield identity mappings, neural networks using orthogonal initialization, and neural-ODE models. Lastly, this paper presents essential design guidelines to promote inherent robustness in deep models, making them more reliable. These recommendations are consistent across all classes of models discussed in this paper. In particular, this paper suggests selecting hyperparameters during training to minimize overfitting rather than avoiding it, encouraging implicit regularization rather than explicit regularization, and designing models to contain malicious interference in a zero-loss area. In line with these suggestions, the proposed RO-NOde model exhibits superior performance. An implementation guide detailing best practices for building robust models can be found at: https://github.com/azazzaa/azazzaa/tree/main

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps of finite composition with dilation vectors of finite length, alongside translation vectors. Unlike translation surfaces, dilation surfaces can possess non-trivial directional flow. We illustrate a dilation surface with a directional flow having no periodic closures. Interestingly, the relation between rank one measurement-preserving subgraphs in dilation surfaces parallels that in translation surfaces. Nevertheless, heterogeneity emerges when examining minimal flow box templates; these may necessitate infinite recursive decomposition. As a consequence, translation surfaces' concepts, such as ultimate recurrence, fail to apply to dilation surfaces. We define the notion of complete coverage in dilation surfaces and demonstrate its equivalence to the abundance of flow preserving 1-to-1 mappings. Derived from this, we define covers of dilation surfaces and the associated translation surfaces. Furthermore, we define dilation covers of rank one, which conform to a specific criteria, known as the Hénon condition. Last, we investigate horizontal intersection numbers in dilation surfaces, providing examples, counterexamples, and proofs of continuity in special instances, like rotation surfaces. Ultimately, we investigate a problem regarding dilation covers of rotation surfaces with a single ingredient, seeking generalizations applicable to various rotation surfaces categories.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as a biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed Correlation Explanation to estimate total correlation and verified the reliability of its estimates and clustering results against established standards. Furthermore, we validated the large scale connectivity network constructed from extensive open fMRI datasets by confirming its alignment with existing neuroscientific knowledge while also revealing additional relationships between brain regions. Lastly, we highlighted the utility of connectivity graphs derived from total correlation in identifying brain diseases. By validating total correlation as a reliable tool, we have developed a novel method for inferring large-scale brain connectivity networks that can be utilized for diagnosing brain diseases. The method may be applied to any available open fMRI dataset with anatomical reconstruction to create a connectivity network, an example of which has been provided in our online repository. A graphical user interface for visually analyzing the generated connectivity network has been made available online. Further research may leverage machine learning methods to diagnose diseases from these connectivity networks. The method used in this study is documented in a publicly accessible repository, located at: https://github.com/Techses/TCforFC.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions through random sampling. Traditional techniques for generating samples from Gaussian process posterior calculations consider samples as separate draws from the distribution of process values at fixed points. This focus on distribution characteristics leads to strategies that increase exponentially with the desired number of points. This becomes impractical for large sets of points, even if the number remains proportional to the data size, which is less than ideal. As an improvement, we propose drawing to the mean, a method that transforms Gaussian process posterior samples into approximate realizations. These samples mimic actual realizations by compensating for errors resulting from approximate random function evaluations, which utilize efficient techniques such as square root and low-rank approximations to maintain scalability. We also provide a guarantee of a specified level of accuracy and validate its effectiveness with empirical tests, specifically in predicting word-level characteristics in written language. Drawing to the mean enables incorporating these characteristics in probabilistic models and improving prediction accuracy, up to 5%, in return for a minor increase in computational cost. Consequently, we suggest using drawing to the mean as an alternative to traditional methods for generating Gaussian process posterior samples based on a predetermined number of points. Additionally, we offer low-rank approximations as a complementary strategy to accelerate Gaussian process inference. This approach is particularly convenient because it does not necessitate explicit drawing from the process, providing a viable alternative for practical applications. Drawing to the mean is now available as an open-source library, ready for use. You can find it at this repository on GitHub. 

A previously published version of this content can be found in the paper "Drawing to the Mean: Gaussian Process Posterior Sampling" on arXiv, Preprint arXiv:2101.07915.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data, specifically known as experience replay. Standard experience replay enables agents to draw upon past knowledge, breaking free from sequential decision-making constraints. However, the classical approach suffers from a major limitation: all past data receive equal consideration. This paper presents a novel concept known as adaptive experience replay, allowing the agent to dynamically weigh different data points according to their relative usefulness. Effective adaptation of past data complexity requires a suitable metric to evaluate both the data's influence and its coverage of the decision-making environment. Here, a versatile, easy-to-implement metric known as the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) metric is presented, offering promising performance and efficient computation. The MLE metric derives its name from its origins in computing the parameter values that best fit a probability distribution model, specifically the Gaussian distribution, to a dataset. In the context of dynamic systems, this parameter represents the optimal noise level, serving as a suitable metric to measure both the data's relevance and its coverage of the Gaussian distribution. As a bonus, the computation of the MLE metric involves the covariance matrix, making it a valuable tool in its own right. The proposed approach, known as adaptive experience replay, is then empirically validated in a series of experiments involving both simple and complex, multi-dimensional systems, demonstrating its benefits and superiority over sequential decision-making strategies, particularly in the optimization of control policies. The results demonstrate that adaptive experience replay can effectively accelerate the optimization of control policies, with the added benefit of making the computation of the MLE metric useful and efficient. Two new strategies have been proposed to apply the supersymmetry method from Gaussian matrices to broader rotation-invariant matrices. Specifically, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula have emerged as viable approaches. By showing the equivalence of these strategies, we aim to demonstrate their common effectiveness, ultimately involving the transformation of supersymmetric matrix integrals into related quadratic supermatrix calculations with defined symmetry constraints. This new approach has the potential to broaden the application of the supersymmetry method to various non-Gaussian matrices, such as those associated with supersymmetric theories in (2+1) dimensions. Furthermore, it is expected that this strategy can facilitate the simplification of complex matrix calculations. Several example applications illustrating the supersymmetry method's extended scope and simplified use will be presented. These include the calculation of supersymmetric partition functions in models featuring flavor dimensions, the derivation of spectral density formulas, and the determination of characteristic properties of flavoured chiral Wigner matrices. Moreover, our findings indicate that the supersymmetric method's scope and efficacy are significantly enhanced when expressed in terms of the supersymmetric (mass) tensor, a concept introduced in this study. Accordingly, this strategy is anticipated to find broad applications in diverse matrix classes. Furthermore, our calculations confirm that the supersymmetric partition function of a general symmetry class can be correctly represented as a quadratic supermatrix determinant, subject to well-defined symmetry constraints. This outcome further underscores the importance of the superbosonization formula in extending the supersymmetry method beyond Gaussian matrices. Lastly, our analysis reveals that the study of superbosonization may also facilitate novel insights and strategies for the reduction of complex matrix calculations. Consequently, this approach has the potential to significantly broaden the applicability and utility of the supersymmetric method in diverse theoretical and applied contexts. This research focuses on bridging the gap between programming languages employing garbage collection for memory management and those leveraging advanced type systems to ensure memory safety in imperative languages. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to ensure safe access to reference types that can be copied, with a particular emphasis on its novel extension to languages with such a typing system, enabling the safe allocation and disposal of cyclic data structures. This work introduces a linear capability that respects the 'copy-on-write' principle and integrates it with an advanced type system to ensure that operations on shared resources are explicit and avoid data races. Furthermore, we propose a garbage collector that mimics the effects of the linear capability, allowing users to collect cyclic data structures that do not compromise the type system's guarantees. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points: (1) under what circumstances do linear co-adding algorithms produce well-defined point spread functions, (2) how do these algorithms relate to nonlinear ones, and (3) what are the necessary conditions for both linear and nonlinear co-adding methods to produce co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. In addition, we discuss how to determine if the co-added point spread function represents the average of individual exposures or is modified during the co-adding process. Our initial analysis focuses on linear combinations of images, including image registration, weight assignment, and combination methods, which enables us to accurately determine the point spread function of each image and thus the co-added image. This knowledge also enables us to make predictions about when linear co-adding algorithms produce well-defined point spread functions. We derive analogous conclusions for nonlinear combinations of images and explore conditions under which both linear and nonlinear co-adding algorithms yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. In particular, we demonstrate that if at least one input image has a well-defined point spread function, then both linear and nonlinear combinations of images result in co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Furthermore, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for both linear and nonlinear combinations of images to result in co-added images with well-defined point spread functions, which differs from previous work. In addition, we derive conditions to preserve flux measurements for linear and nonlinear combinations of images, which differs from previous work. Our analysis suggests that preserving flux measurements is challenging, especially when combining images with different point spread functions. Our results also imply that preserving flux measurements using nonlinear combinations of images requires these weights to be one, which represents averaging images. This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in these solids must comply with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. A critical premise is that the fracture of a solid initiates when the apex of a pre-existing notch reaches a critical instability point, beyond which it begins to sharpen uncontrollably. The resulting predictions derived from this analysis were tested and validated against the meticulous measurements conducted by Gumbsch and associates, who examined the notch toughness of predeformed and non-deformed tungsten crystals under various conditions, spanning a wide range of temperatures, loading rates, and initial states. Notably, the theoretical framework's quantitative predictions consistently aligned with the experimental findings, covering both types of fracture and encompassing different thermal conditions and initial dislocation densities. This exceptional quantitative agreement underscores the thermodynamic theory's soundness and provides compelling evidence for its underlying notion that the fracture instability revolves around a pivotal change in the dislocation's configuration within the solid crystal. Furthermore, the theoretical framework's adaptability enables it to anticipate and account for the remarkable phenomenon commonly known as "grain-bridgetoughness," which manifests in the intergranular fracture of materials characterized by low dislocation mobility. In such instances, the fracture spares microscopic clusters of dislocations accumulated at the grain boundaries rather than propagating through the material along a nonlinear trajectory. This prediction regarding "grain-bridgetoughness" not only aligns with earlier observational findings but also underscores the interplay between crack tip processes and the material's microscopic resilience at the grain level. Ultimately, the theoretical framework's insights into the fracture toughness of solid crystals at a microscopic level challenge conventional notions and lay bare the shortcomings of existing theories, while also suggesting a deeper connection between strength, work-hardening rates, and the material's defect structure. This quantitative framework's potential applications extend beyond understanding static fracture by anticipating that the same thermodynamic principles governing crack propagation should also influence the solid's response to rapid changes in temperature, dynamic loading, and the intricate interplay between mechanical and thermal stresses, all while remaining robust in the face of nonlinear elastic deformations. A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem, where its applications extend beyond digital currencies. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, specifically in the context of a physical internet, a novel blockchain design has been proposed. This design incorporates lazy verification, batched transaction authentication, and batched block verification, aiming to reduce processing time and energy consumption. Specifically, the lazy verification mechanism minimizes energy consumption by limiting the number of computations per node, the batched transaction authentication reduces processing time by minimizing the number of transactions per block, and batched block verification decreases the number of block verifications per node. Simulated results show that the proposed blockchain achieves faster finalization times and reduced energy consumption compared to existing solutions. This novel design outperforms the existing blockchain systems in a physical internet setting and can be directly integrated into IoT devices without dependence on central authorities. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized by screen readers. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an approach based on autoregressive language modeling. XLNet can capture bidirectional contexts without the limitations of input masking and outperforms BERT across various downstream tasks. Moreover, XLNet's use of autoregressive context modeling enables it to effectively model temporal positional dependencies, which enhances its ability to handle tasks involving temporal contexts, such as machine reading comprehension and question answering. Interestingly, we discovered that augmenting BERT with autoregressive pretraining improves BERT's bidirectional pretraining performance, suggesting that autoregressive modeling can be utilized as a method for enhancing BERT models. Consequently, we developed ERNIE-DP, a new model that synergizes denoising autoencoding with autoregressive pretraining to achieve improved performance over BERT and XLNet. Furthermore, our model's use of duplicating inputs in autoregressive pretraining facilitates the modeling of positional dependencies, enriching its ability to handle various downsteam tasks. When fine-tuned, our model, BERT-DP, yields superior performance to BERT and XLNet across multiple tasks. Notably, our model overcomes several limitations of BERT and BERT-based models and offers a viable approach to enhancing BERT models. Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large, distant galaxies that are too faint to be seen in UV imaging taken by the Hubble Space Telescope. Using high-resolution mid-infrared images taken by the Advanced Camera for Surveys on board the Hubble Space Telescope, a new sample of 15 faint galaxies was identified, along with an existing subset of 15 faint galaxies selected based on their near-infrared and submillimeter properties. This combined subset of 30 galaxies was then analyzed using a two-stage clustering method to examine their physical properties. This analysis suggested that the majority of these galaxies were highly inclined and have red infrared colors, although some of these galaxies may have interacted with other stars or molecular gas before being observed in their current state. The mass of the stars within these galaxies was also found to be significantly limited, although some individual galaxies did show evidence of having formed many thousands of new stars at an incredible rate. A final model suggested that the vast majority of the individual stars within these galaxies have not yet been observed to emit light in the UV spectrum, which places strict limitations on the rate at which these galaxies form new stars. This suggests that the individual stars within these galaxies are primarily buried deep within large amounts of dust, while their host galaxies are largely obscured from our view. This container is sealed by movable walls that can be adjusted, thereby permitting the displacement of the walls to influence fluid dynamics. As a result, a system seeking equilibrium is formed by variously jammed positions, characterized by different arrangements of the heavier disks. This study applies the concept of a unique family of weights to describe these configurations. This family serves as a generalization of the well-known "riddle of the harp" system, thereby offering a broader understanding of the equilibrium states in this horizontal container. Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often using a linear model which assumes consistent statistical dependencies across various ENSO phases, a notion not necessarily supported. We estimate the time-dependent co-occurrence probabilities of significant precipitation anomalies with both East Pacific and Central Pacific El Ni\~no using a hidden Markov model that accommodates dynamic changes. The analysis provides a clear picture of the distinct impacts of each flavor on global precipitation patterns, revealing a complex interplay where one flavor can suppress the other's effects, a phenomenon observed in parts of Asia during Central Pacific El Ni\~no events. Notably, the effects of East Pacific El Ni\~no on the Indonesian region and those of Central Pacific El Ni\~no on Australia and East Africa appear to be stronger than those associated with East Pacific El Ni\~no globally. We develop a conceptual model that uses geographical considerations and atmospheric circulation patterns like monsoons to explain these findings. The different climate responses to the two flavors may offer opportunities for improved short-term precipitation forecasts and more effective risk management strategies in regions heavily influenced by precipitation. We identify additional avenues for exploration and gather evidence that highlights the need for statistical models to capture dynamic changes in climate variability data. In materials lacking internal order, applied mechanical stress often leads to uneven deformation, which distort's the material's spatial framework in ways that cannot be uniformly described. Typically, researchers characterize this distortion by relating local deformation rates to nearby neighbor distances; however, a recently proposed approach (Radin et al., 2016) instead relies on a comprehensive analysis of the deforming structure's topological features, specifically the generation of rings within this lattice. This paper provides a detailed mathematical explanation of this proposed model and derives precise key metrics that describe the transition from linear to nonlinear deformation within these disordered materials. These metrics are tested using data from three distinct models representing rigid, soft, and deformable spherical particles dispersed within a medium. Importantly, this study reveals a significant distinction in the topological features at the initial stages of deformation between materials that are nearly rigid and those that are more pliable. The derived equations also enable the direct comparison of the rate of topological ring formation under stress in rigid and soft particle systems, thereby quantifying mechanical response differences between these dispersions and traditional solid materials. Overall, this research demonstrates the feasibility of using precise, comprehensive topological features to track the gradual degradation of material rigidity and to develop a deeper understanding of the role of topological features in ultimate material failure. Additionally, these methods may hold promise for gaining insights into the complex mechanical properties of living cells. The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with certain weakening and contraction properties. This achievement builds on a previous result regarding the contraction counterparts of these extensions, while the computational complexity was not determined for them. In this study, we introduce just the necessary concepts related to well-quasi-orderings and fast-growing complexity classes, enabling us to provide upper bounds on complexity for the extensions in question. This outcome particularly provides a solution to an open problem in the fuzzy logic community by offering a specific complexity bound for MTL. We also provide an illustration of our approach by re-examining the model completion concept in the context of MTL. Furthermore, we establish that a particular set of substructural logics possessing a form of mixed weakening, whose language includes bunched implications, also exhibits decidability. This achievement encompasses, inter alia, the axiomatic extension of classical relevance logic with de Morgan exponentiation. The logics in question are formulated over a specific language containing left- and right-distributive operators, whose behavior can be compared to their analogs in classical logic. We leverage our general framework, developed for first-order substructural logic, to leverage a general decidability result. Additionally, we provide semantic characterizations for the first-order counterparts of these extensions, making them part of a broader class of representable substructural logics. We establish that certain axioms governing above-bounded distributivity allow the model theory of their first-order counterparts to be compared to that of relevance arithmetic, its expanded version for first-order logic. We establish the model companionship of these first-order extensions, making them amenable to a semantic characterization, thereby providing a novel instance of the model completion concept in the context of substructural logics. We establish a specific complexity bound for the decidability of the underlying first-order logic, thereby providing an upper bound that closely resembles the complexity of relevance arithmetic, its expanded version for first-order logic. We further establish that certain key theorems, such as the compactness theorem, cut-elimination, the completeness theorem, and the zero-one compactness theorem, hold for these extensions. Finally, we provide an illustration of our approach by applying our results on MTL to provide a solution to an open problem in the fuzzy logic community. We establish the model companionship of MTL and provide a semantic characterization of its model class, thereby providing an alternative proof of its compactness theorem and the zero-one compactness theorem. Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research has sought to automatically enhance taxonomies by learning concept representations in Euclidean space. However, the natural hierarchical structure and rich geometric structure of hyperbolic space make it a more suitable platform for representation. We propose HyperExpan, an framework that generates hyperbolic representations of concepts to facilitate informed decision-making during taxonomy expansion. HyperExpan employs a hyperbolic graph neural network to preserve hierarchical relationships and a hyperbolic probe to adapt to the dynamic taxonomy. Experiment results demonstrate that HyperExpan surpasses the performance of existing methods based in Euclidean space. Additionally, HyperExpan's representation of concepts is characterized by improved accuracy and interpretability. We show that HyperExpan's representation can effectively distinguish between synonymous and homonymous concepts. Importantly, HyperExpan's representations are stable and resilient to category shifts similar to those encountered in real-world applications. We verify the effectiveness of HyperExpan's representations through a case study on a taxonomy of dentistry, where these representations accurately capture the nuances of new dental specialties that are unknown to the model. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in environmental factors and operator subjectivity often go unaccounted for in decision-making, causing shipment delays and inaccuracies in budget projections. This widespread issue demands correction, and existing approaches have explored solutions via stochastic or fuzzy logic models. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for quantifying non-deterministic uncertainty through probabilistic modeling, which is universally applicable to various industrial datasets. Probabilistic modeling offers several benefits, such as flexibility in modeling various uncertainty types and facilitating distribution manipulation. By applying probabilistic modeling to real-world datasets from the textile and diving industries, we examine non-linear transformations and their effects on discrete schedules and evaluate the proposed method's performance relative to traditional methods. Our comparative analysis demonstrates the proposed approach's superiority in recognizing uncertainty patterns and producing more realistic models compared to other methods. Extensive simulation testing verifies that optimal solutions derived using the proposed approach frequently yield lower costs and delays while ensuring feasible schedules, whereas traditional methods may result in infeasible schedules due to increased uncertainty. This research outlines a novel and effective technique for addressing complex uncertainty in real-world industrial settings and highlights its potential for widespread applicability in various industrial environments. Furthermore, it provides a practical methodology for leveraging big data analytics to enhance visibility and quality in industrial production.
