Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated through the use of case studies, marking a breakthrough in understanding multi-dimensional resiliency semantics. The associated theory is made available online at https://github.com/msadaghi/RSRV. Additionally, this research expands the field of multi-objective monitoring of STL formulas, previously explored in [Kemmner et al., 2020]. Although our work is initially applied to CPS systems, it is universally applicable to any complex system requiring resiliency assessment. Further investigation of our algorithm's time complexity is scheduled for future research, albeit with initially elevated expenses due to its non-polymorphic complexity, as evidenced by its dependency on the size of the transition matrix even for polyomial STL formulas. As shown in section 6, this leads to an exponential complexity problem for linear STL formulas. Nevertheless, we believe that this framework serves as a robust foundation for future optimizations. The underlying code has been made publicly available on https://github.com/msagir/RSVL. This research received funding from the Swiss National Science Foundation project P2FP (SNSF 170021-146613). One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and axion quark nuggets, employing accelerometers in a network configuration and discusses how atomic interferometry-based networks might enhance these searches. Although atomic interferometry has limitations, such a network could significantly improve the detection limits of accelerometer-based searches, particularly for dark matter particles weighing over keV. This article also outlines the current state of experiments and future searches using deep submicron CMOS sensors, standard interferometry, and precision laser Michelson interferometry, showcasing the vast potential of atomic interferometry in the search for dark matter. Finally, we examine prospective applications beyond dark matter detection, such as quantum-based dark matter detection and sensitivity enhancement, and discuss how atomic interferometry-based networks could contribute to this field. Additionally, we explore potential applications and drawbacks of such a network, including its utility in dark matter research, quantum-based dark matter detection, and sensitivity enhancement, and discuss how atomic interferometry-based networks might help overcome current limitations in dark matter detection. Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. The implications are that significant polarization signals from smaller radio sources may be missed in large survey databases, affecting intergalactic plasma studies and CMB background estimation. Further, significant polarization from large radio sources might also go undetected due to corresponding spectral curvature. Correcting for this bias will be crucial for accurately measuring the intergalactic plasma signal in the foreground. Based on the current data, about 8% of radio galaxies below ~2nJy are expected to have significant polarization. However, due to resolution thresholds in these surveys, only ~0.6% of ~2nJy sources per square degree are expected to have notable polarization. Therefore, to determine the plasma signal with sufficient precision, future studies need to improve in several key areas, including enhanced sensitivity, better instrumentation, more precise calibration, and a more sophisticated modeling approach that accounts for complex effects like GMRT polarization and a possible change in the plasma signal background. Alongside these considerations, it is also essential to carefully analyze the population of radio sources with high polarization in detail, rather than simply subtracting them from the analysis, due to the potential for unique astrophysical signals from these sources. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation. In contrast to the existing literature, we emphasize that turbulent transport cannot be fully described through a diffusivity tensor alone; instead, a more comprehensive description is necessary, particularly for flows involving multiple channels and counter-currents. Our findings are supported by a three-dimensional simulation of flow around a pair of interacting vortex rings, which we use to demonstrate the inability of the local diffusion tensor to accurately model the associated transport processes. By modeling these flows as continuous time Markov processes, we are able to quantify the turbulent transport properties based solely on the intensity of the flow. Moreover, our results reveal that the critical adjustment for localized modeling of turbulent transport lies in the adjustment factor $e^{\tau^2}$, with $\tau$ representing the time scale of transition between coherent structures and the characteristic time for adjustment of material layers within those structures. Furthermore, by modeling turbulent transport as a Markov process allows for the recovery of a separate class of transport properties along particular paths, analogous to the $q$-correlator in existing literature. In conclusion, our study significantly enhances the existing models for turbulent transport by ideally merging two long-standing approaches - the stochastic advection problem and the approximation of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor - resulting in a more precise description and numerical estimation of turbulent transport properties. Moreover, our methodology can be conveniently integrated into existing numerical simulations, such as those used in recent studies on the material transfer between vortex rings. As an example of its applicability, our methodology has been used to generate three-dimensional simulation data for the continuous time Markov process modeling of turbulent transport properties. This data, along with the accompanying code and results, is available online at a publicly accessible repository. Ultimately, our study aims to contribute to future advancements in the field by addressing novel questions and challenges related to the transport of matter across diverse coherent flows, thereby opening doors to the exploration of multiple scales within these flows. Phenomenological models are essential for understanding the underlying physics, but they must be grounded in relevant theories. We suggest that nuclear elastic scattering is best evaluated by first employing a simple, general theory, then refining it with model parameters to match data. Using this approach, we re-evaluated the $^{4}$He + $^{12}$C, $^{28}$Si, $^{40}$Ca, and $^{56}$Fe scattering, identifying key insights: 1) an unexpected minimum exists in the optical potential at non-zero energies; 2) non-zero, positive volume potentials are required to match data below 20 MeV; 3) a unique, case-by-case surface potential is needed; 4) comparative evaluations of the various systems can offer fresh insights into nuclear physics. In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems. These innovative algorithms work within a unified framework that leverages an established approach for generating discrete uniform random variables through bit-scouted a-bobba distributions. As a by-product, we also create new algorithms for solving the well-known broadcast and consensus problems in single-hop beeping networks. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the developed counting algorithm surpasses previous results (Detrich et al., 2021) by offering a significantly reduced processing time. Analysis of the developed algorithms considers their overall performance, averaging, and worst-case scenarios to establish reliable complexity assessments. Expanding the scope of our work, we consider extensions to multi-hop beeping networks and examine the additional complexity introduced by these distributed communication systems. Interestingly, our results show that both naming and counting problems in such networks face increased complexity due to the presence of multiple hops. Comprehensive simulation experiments are performed to verify the efficiency of our proposed algorithms and determine their performance in various network settings. The source code for the developed algorithms has been made available on GitHub. As a significant achievement, our results reveal that beeping networks can execute the distributed learning framework of [Malkin et al. 2022] efficiently in just O(n) rounds, thanks to our proposed counting algorithm. In a fascinating extension, we discovered that naming and counting problems in beeping networks can be represented as combinatorial optimization problems within graph theory and, consequently, solved using greedy algorithms. However, our results show that such a linear approach results in significantly increased processing time and energy usage at the cost of sacrificing randomness. Ultimately, our proposed counting algorithm offers a superior alternative, achieving a more efficient solution to the naming problem by adopting a linear approach. multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. We now have 
numerous techniques to compile datasets without explicitly identifying these 
switchpoints, enabling researchers to explore novel methods for code-mixed word 
embedding training. This study presents an innovative technique to learn 
representations for mixed languages without relying on external resources,

character transitions. Comparing our approach to four state-of-the-art methods

languages at a lower computational cost. Furthermore, our study includes 
detailed experiments with a newly developed code-mixed dataset. The trained 
embeddings and code are publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at higher pressures, suggesting the importance of its van Hove singularities in superconducting H3S compounds. Moreover, we found that the density of states strongly influences the crossover between the two interactions, causing the electron-electron interaction to dominate at low pressures and the electron-phonon interaction to dominate at high pressures. Overall, our results highlight the significance of incorporating the variable density of states into calculations to gain insights into both interactions and predict experimental outcomes more accurately. The findings also emphasize that H3S is comprised of simple CsCl-bonded LaAlO3 units with varying interatomic distances, as supported by microscopic calculations at high pressures. The resulting phase diagram shows three distinct phases with a reentrant behavior, where the SC phase reappears between two inscribed lobes. The density of states shows distinct peaks at 162 and 204 GPa, corresponding to transitions between SC and insulating phases. The former occurs as H3S transitions from a hypothesized H2S-like state to a SC state, while the latter marks a transition to a H2S-like state, both of which are hypothesized to occur at 162 and 204 GPa, respectively. The variable density of states significantly influences these transitions and the SC instability, underscoring the necessity of incorporating it to forecast experimental outcomes and understand both interactions. The approach and methodology employed in this study can be applied to future superconducting materials to achieve a deeper understanding of their complexity. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine 6-DoF camera poses by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve high accuracy under both real-world and simulated scenarios. Moreover, this method's performance is further validated through successful application to the Challenge 1 subtasks of the TASC 2020 challenge. The implementation of this technique, including its code and pre-trained models, is made accessible through a public repository for ease of replication. The specific repository can be found at: https://github.com/amberwangskylab/MSRF. Furthermore, the paper develops an optimization technique, leveraging the dual problem of the LASSO optimization, to efficiently calculate the maximum achievable sum-rate performance. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. This research is primarily motivated by a study published in 2015, where a conditionally asymptotically negligible Markov chain was developed as a model for a class of bio-statistical models. As an additional contribution, we verify the uniform convergence of a non-homogeneous Markov process toward its quasi-stationary equilibrium. This outcome has potential applications in bio-statistics, as well as other fields of engineering and physics. Unfortunately, we are unable to prove a uniform convergence bound for a general, stationary Markov process toward its quasi-stationary equilibrium. However, we establish that if the QSE of a Markov process exhibits continuous dependence on its transition rates, then a Markov process attaining a self-consistent, ergodic QSE will converge uniformly toward that equilibrium at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. This research further suggests a novel relationship between quasistationary equilibrium distribution and the principal eigenfunctions of a Markov process transition matrix, which we have termed "QSE eigenfunctions." Furthermore, we evaluate whether forthcoming facilities, like the High-Luminosity LHC, the Circular Electron Positron Collider, the International Linear Collider, and the Future Circular Collider, electron edition will be capable of probing two Higgs doublet model parameters. This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the stationary Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input forces and resulting flows in dimension d. This work shows that the stationary Navier-Stokes equation becomes unstable when the input forces decrease slowly with spatial frequencies for certain dimensions and types of flows, causing the solution map to diverge at zero. Conversely, we find that this divergence is not a concern when the input forces decrease rapidly, and we specifically identify cases where this holds true for 3D and 4D systems. By employing sophisticated mathematical techniques such as functional analysis and approximate compactness, we reprove wellposedness for the stationary Navier-Stokes equation in 4D and establish a new result for 3D systems, where we demonstrate that the solution map is continuously differentiable under a certain range of conditions. Notably, this result contributes towards resolving an open question from the 2019 paper. On the other hand, we also prove that the solution map diverges in certain dimensions and wave types, and we show that this divergence occurs even if the system is controlled, which provides a negative answer to a question raised by Wu and Tsurumi in 2020. Moreover, we give an example of a 4D system where the solution map diverges when given certain types of forces, which directly addresses Tsurumi's question. To achieve these results, we develop a new approximation method for Navier-Stokes equations that generalizes a technique from Wu and Tsurumi in a consistent way, and we also establish a general stability criterion for solution maps that is applied universally across different types of equations, which reflects our findings. We ultimately aim to generalize our results to more complex systems and theoretical Navier-Stokes models, which would be a significant breakthrough towards understanding these equations. Long document retrieval has been a longstanding hurdle in both reading comprehension and information retrieval. Recent pre-training models have shown promise in addressing this challenge, particularly in the retrieval and ranking stages of long documents. Nonetheless, issues persist in the realm of long document retrieval, such as the challenge of precisely identifying the relevant text segment within a long document and differentiating it from irrelevant information. In our research, we investigate how contrastive learning can be effectively applied at the passage level to enhance long document retrieval. Subsequently, we introduce a novel dataset consisting of over 9,000 questions and 38,000 annotated passages, designed to streamline the deployment of reading comprehension models on legal platforms. Our proposed reading comprehension pipeline achieves outstanding performance on this new dataset, earning a pass rate of 83.1% and outperforming current state-of-the-art models in both recall and precision metrics. Crucially, our findings indicate that contrastive learning can significantly improve the recall rate by 6.2% and pass rate by 6.6%. The source code, dataset, and trained models will be publicly accessible on GitHub.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with a class-balanced adaptation in our proposed framework. Experimental results demonstrate that InfoGNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in pseudo-labeling and associated semi-supervised GNN training. Moreover, it exhibits exceptional robustness in scenarios with extensive pseudo-label noise and severe class imbalance. A thorough analysis of the proposed method's components further underscores its advanced performance characteristics. The source code of InfoGNN is made publicly available at https://github.com/leverle/InfoGNN. Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the initial conditions of an accelerated electron bunch affect the resulting betatron radiation spectra. It is found that the spectroscopy can differentiate between cold and heated electron distributions, as well as distinguish between over- and under-shoots in the X-ray peak intensity. For an axisymmetric plasma structure, the phenomenon of electron spin is considered, revealing that left- and right-handed circular polarized radiation emit from oppositely spinning electrons. Consequently, the spectroscopy may reveal the handedness of the electron bunch's initial conditions, a property influenced by the electron injection technique. If the plasma is axisymmetric but contains azimuthal asymmetry in the electron density, the spectroscopy can identify the handedness of this electron distribution. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for performing SGD (CA-SGD), which reduces the overall communication expenditure to a minimum. This is achieved by organizing the computation in a way that minimizes the frequency and quantity of data exchange between computation and communication operations. Our analysis reveals a communication cost for CA-SGD of O(n * log(n)) in a given batch setting, which significantly outperforms standard SGD and other optimization methods like SDAG and ASGD by lowering communication frequency. Moreover, our technique surpasses broadcast-based approaches such as SDAG and ASGD in communication quantity. To evaluate the efficiency of our technique, we conducted extensive testing using a batch execution of SGD on various data sets with different processes, our results show a up to 93.5% reduction in communication cost compared to broadcast-based methods, paired with a 84.3% decrease in communication frequency when compared to batch-free execution. Lastly, our technique allows for its performance to directly compete with optimization methods that circumvent communication altogether, revealing that in some instances communication avoidance comes at the expense of computation inefficiency. To facilitate our methodology's reproduction, the associated code and guides for our technique have been made publicly available on the public code repository at https://github.com/parallelml/ca-sgd. Additionally, our technique's accompanying documentation and guides for our technique have been made publicly available at http://parallelml.github.io. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used by investment strategists and analysts to analyze financial trends and make predictions. However, with the emergence of advanced machine learning techniques, especially generative adversarial networks from computer vision and graphics, there has been a recent shift towards using these models for time series simulation in financial analysis. Current markov-chain based generative models like the conditional generative adversarial network can only achieve success when given extensive knowledge of prior time series data. Nevertheless, in real-world financial analysis this is often impractical due to unavailability of long-term historical data. As a result, the primary goal of this paper is to propose a new model that integrates features from both conditional variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks to effectively simulate time series data. This model leverages a structured encoding and decoding mechanism utilizing a directed acyclic graph to encode the temporal characteristics of a sequence. Furthermore, the utility of the simulated data from this model has been demonstrated in a semi-markets simulation setting to teach the Markowitz model a robust diversification strategy. With this approach, the simulation can be used in sampling different investment datasets for a portfolio under various market conditions. Experimental outcomes show that the utility of the simulated data in this model has been supported by significant statistical analysis. The results of the model's semi-markets simulations reveal a robust diversification strategy that surpasses traditional Markowitz methods, notable in both simulated and real-world market conditions. The proposed model has significant potential to offer an advantageous platform for time series analysis in financial trends prediction. Comprehensive detail of the model, including implementation, the directed acyclic graph structure, loss functions, the Markowitz model, and semi-markets simulations, has been made accessible in the source code available on GitHub. Furthermore, the efficacy of the proposed model has been evaluated through several benchmark tests against traditional generative models like the conditional generative adversarial network and variational autoencoder in both semi-markets and markov-chain settings. The outcomes show that the proposed model has attained state-of-the-art results in both settings, a considerable enhancement over current generative models like the conditional generative adversarial network. Moreover, the proposed model has significantly improved sampling efficiency using the variational autoencoder, a notable advancement over previous markov-chain based generative models. The previous autoencoding model for time series has also been refined, incorporating an integrated structure to effectively sample a sequence while preserving both temporal and casual properties. In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation, which we term the tensor join. This operation allows us to identify novel hypergraph properties and prove that many well-known hypergraph characteristics can be formulated in terms of the tensor join. To maximize computational efficiency, we recommend an adaptive strategy for determining hypergraph parameters. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the tensor join's inputs when a hypergraph's property is non-trivial. Finally, we outline two areas where the tensor join is expected to be particularly useful. Firstly, it will facilitate the introduction of new hypergraph parameters by translating existing parameter definitions to tensor-based forms. Secondly, it will enable the computation of these parameters to achieve faster calculation times. To quantify the computational advantages of our approach, we consider the task of counting the closed hypergraphs contained in a given hypergraph, demonstrating that this parameter has a non-trivial definition in terms of the tensor join and yielding a novel, efficient algorithm for solving this problem. By employing our system of hypergraphs based on the tensor join, we show that this problem can be solved in linear time with respect to the number of hyperedges. To the best of our knowledge, this result represents a novel, efficient solution to the problem of counting the closed hypergraphs contained in a given hypergraph. Our approach also extends to more specialized classes of hypergraphs, such as q-uniform hypergraphs, where q is a prime number. In this context, we discover that the tensor join facilitates a non-trivial definition of the hypergraph's property of being a Turán limit, thereby enabling the computation of this property in linear time. Our code for implementing the ideas presented in this paper is openly available on the Platform for Advanced Data Science Analytics. With this code, users can reproduce the results of our experiments and perform new calculations by specifying input parameters. Our code can be accessed through the following link: https://datastories.uio.no/platform/project/view/220. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. To mitigate this limitation, this paper explores the use of time as a continuous variable, clustering correlated observations over specific intervals, a method that is evaluated through simulations and case studies. The method is compared to traditional models via concordance coefficients and graphical analysis. The results suggest that modeling time as continuous with clustered data offers a viable alternative to the repeated measures model, particularly when dealing with categorical time. The associated R package, clinCCRM, is also introduced, which accommodates various extensions to the repeated measures model. The package's flexibility is reflected in its support for various fixed effects, non-normal error distributions, and a version of the repeated measures model that factors in the dying process, particularly when dealing with terminal disease patients. The implementation of the proposed method is further reinforced by theoretical convergence tests. The terminal effect model has been added to the popular R package, clinFunnel, which originally supports the standard repeated measures model. The combined packages offer a robust tool for analyzing data from clinical funnels with correlated repeated measures, particularly when dealing with time-dependent covariates. The proposed method is illustrated through two case studies, involving data from patients with Alzheimer's and cancer, tracked over time. The performance of the proposed method is also compared to standard mixed models through simulations and case studies, revealing the superiority of the repeated measures model, whether continuous or categorical. The open-source resources, including the R packages and input data, are available on the GitHub platform. The URLs for the resources are provided in the concluding section. The proposed method has the potential to expand the applicability of the repeated measures model, particularly when dealing with time-dependent covariates, which may offer improved analytical power. The implementation of the proposed method is relatively straightforward, making it accessible to analysts who are familiar with the repeated measures model. The expansion of the proposed method to accommodate non-gaussian error distributions and the dying process is also presented as an alternative, providing additional versatility. The results of the simulations and case studies suggest that the proposed method can enhance analytical power over the repeated measures model. The theoretical convergence tests have the potential to further enhance analytical power by accurately modeling the study design. The proposed method has identified areas for potential improvement and will be expanded to handle even more complex study designs.

The identical symbol is utilized for both conditional measure and Lions derivatives, though context will distinguish whether it represents a conditional measure or a Lions derivative. The identical symbol is utilized for both stochastic integrals, determinants, and other multi-type variables, though context will distinguish whether it represents an integral, logarithmic, or multi-type determinant. We conduct a series of experiments focused on measuring the amount of entanglement in various families of two-qubit two-photon states, using visibility measurements of quantum correlations to achieve the highest possible precision. This paper generalizes the principles of spectral inf-mutual information, previously developed for single-user channels, to more complex systems like interference channels and multi-user channels. It establishes the key properties of these generalized quantities and demonstrates their close connection to well-established channel capacity theorems. Furthermore, it examines how they provide useful bounds on channel capacity when establishing achievable regions under various decoding methods. The investigation reveals that inf-mutual information bounds remain valid even in cases where the channel capacity formula is unknown, such as for the Gaussian disk channel. Ultimately, it shows that the upper limits on inf-mutual information successfully pinpoint the true channel capacity in cases where the channel is memoryless and independently identically distributed. However, for channels with encoded transmissions, even though inf-mutual information overestimates the capacity, it fails to accurately capture decoded interference that is essential for determining reliable transmission rates. As a result, it does not successfully pinpoint the true channel capacity in such scenarios. This research also explores the inf-mutual information of multi-user channels and reveals that the properties of entangled observables may offer insights into optimizing transmission rates in such complex systems. Consequently, future works could utilize the established connections and properties of entangled observables as a means to further bound multi-user channel capacity. Moreover, the idea that inf-mutual information provides an optimal bound on channel capacity even when the channel is not memoryless sparks the possibility of finding similar generalizations for other channel capacity bounds like the cut-back channel capacity theorem. Lastly, the research delves into the theoretical ramifications of having infinitely many degrees of freedom when the channel is not memoryless, which may significantly impact data security. In particular, it is found that data interference can be entangled, which may significantly decrease data safety. This highlights the significance of having a reliable decoding method to counter such entangled interference. Future works could utilize the established connections and properties of entangled observables to further study this entangled interference, entangled interference interference, and develop methods to counter it. Consequently, the research also offers an alternative understanding of the interference channel capacity through its connection to the interference in mutual information, which may provide new insights into achievable decoding methods. In particular, the study reveals that the interference in mutual information provides an inf-mutual information bound on interference channel capacity from below. Consequently, the study offers an entangled observables-based model of interference entropy, which may also offer new insights into achievable decoding methods in such channels. Ultimately, the research explores an entangled observables-based model

The timely detection of COVID-19 can help minimize the risk of severe illness, protect at-risk individuals, and alleviate the surge in healthcare systems. Detecting the disease as early as possible through the use of symptoms is crucial. There's been a scarcity of data on COVID-19 symptom onset in Ireland, which is why collecting and publishing COVID- reported symptoms from the start of the disease are essential. Using the Dublin COVID-19 Surveillance report, we compiled a dataset of daily cases categorized by symptom presence and status from March 2020 to March 2021. With 1,946 cases, we present this new data, which we believe will contribute to research on detecting the disease at its early stages. Our findings include periodic patterns in symptom prevalence and a higher incidence of positive cases with symptoms, particularly in individuals over 60 and with pre-existing health conditions. This data has the potential to improve the detection of COVID-19 using machine learning techniques, particularly for individuals with mild or no symptoms. To facilitate further research, we've made the data available through the DataEnclave, TCD, and the DataAssist platforms. Research collaborators can register to access the data. Our early-detection research is ongoing and we plan to continuously update the dataset as new cases emerge. Our work is focused on training machine learning models to detect the disease at its early stages and we invite research collaborators to register their interest. Registration will provide access to the data and the opportunity to connect with our research team. Our ultimate goal is to train algorithms to detect the disease at its early stages, facilitating precise and timely diagnosis. This, in turn, is essential for informing individuals, healthcare systems, and the broader community about COVID-19 detection. Our research is being conducted under the aegis of the TESS programme, which focuses on supporting pandemic-relevant research, and is being driven by the surge in COVID-19 infections in Ireland and the scarcity of data on detecting the disease at its early stages. Our work has implications for future infectious diseases that may require monitoring and diagnosing at an early stage, a situation that could arise with a similar prevalence and symptomality to COVID-19. This research is being driven by the generosity of the SFI, TSSG, and the School of Computer Science at University College Dublin, who are supporting our work. Our findings demonstrate that our data can be utilized for training machine learning models to detect the disease at its early stages, facilitating precise and timely diagnosis. Our research is being conducted under the aegis of the DataEnclave

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network model that operates on graph data, extensively applied across various domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can handle complex relationships between data inputs, but its direct use in wireless communication systems is restricted due to the dynamic nature of wireless environments. This dynamicity causes inherent inconsistencies in labeled data, negatively impacting the performance of GNN. Additionally, the unbalanced nature of data, leading to the problem of data inhomogeneity, further compromises GNN's efficiency in graph-based tasks. This work addresses these issues by introducing a weighted graph learning technique to adaptively adjust the edge weights between adjacent nodes. By utilizing a learned edge weighting scheme, the balance problem is effectively resolved, and the influence of each node is modulated to accommodate the uneven data distribution. This approach enables the adaptation of GNN to various communication systems, including those with diverse system designs, inter-node relationships, and wireless channel properties. Specifically, this method is applied to a real-world scenario - 6G metropolitan indoor propagation graph - to validate its efficacy. Our results demonstrate that the proposed edge weighting strategy significantly enhances the accuracy of GNN by up to 12.6% over traditional models. According to the computational requirements, the proposed method incurs only a minor performance cost, increasing the training time by about 10%. Our research aims to inspire the next-generation wireless networks to integrate with emerging technologies like neuroscience-inspired signal processing, to create innovative end-to-end network architectures that can handle diverse network and wireless channel dynamics. This work has the potential to empower the next-generation wireless networks to adapt to various system designs, inter-node relationships, and inter-signal dependencies by rising above traditional GNN-based homography. This work can be extended in the following two directions: first, the development of a gradient-based edge weighting scheme might not always converge to a meaningful solution; second, the proposed weighted graph learning approach can be utilized in other GNN applications beyond what is demonstrated here. Therefore, there is a need to ensure the stability of the proposed edge weighting strategy under various graph topologies and GNN applications. This work aims to address these concerns by investigating the convergence behavior of the proposed method. By analyzing the eigenvalue spectrum of the graph Laplacian matrix, we can evaluate the proposed edge weighting method's ability to modulate the spectral properties of the adapted graph. Our results show that the proposed approach enables fine-tuning of the spectral spectrum to alleviate the issues of incomplete label problem. This effect, however, might not be noticeable

In the broader South American context, Brazil ranks third for its homicide death toll behind only Venezuela and Colombia.  In assessing the consequences of violent acts, an analysis of both public health systems and the country's justice systems is required in addition to other essential components. paths algorithm applying SGD with exponentially decreasing step-sizes from $\tau=1 
\to \tau \rightarrow \tau^{\alpha}$ where $\alpha \in [0,1)$. For instance, $\alpha=0.1$

o(1)}+\log T)$ and individual tracking errors of $T$ with high probability. For convex 
objectives, our algorithm also reaches an o(1) tracking error without logarithmic terms. 
Furthermore, our method requires no a-priori knowledge of $\sigma$, $M$ or $\beta$, nor does

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, specifically in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated in the early Universe.  For decades, numerous axion searches have been executed utilizing the electron photon vertex through the process of two-photon interactions, resulting in an array of successful observations with the intention of identifying these antiparticle-like particles.  However, utilizing photons from astrophysical sources presents a novel method for observing ALPs, allowing us to explore previously unattainable parameter space beyond the reach of other methods.  In this study, we examine the potential for scaling ALP searches via photon observations by analyzing the performance requirements of upcoming photometric telescopes such as the Roman Space Telescope, finding that romantic photo ALP searches hold considerable potential using this approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that romantic photo ALP searches may soon probe parameter spaces relevant to the cosmological production of ALPs, a finding previously connected to dark matter. As a result, we propose that cosmic ALP observations should be regarded as an effective means of investigating these dark matter-related regions. In particular, we test this idea by examining the potential for cosmic ALP dark matter correlations using mock observations of the romanic photo ALP dark matter phenomenon with the romanic space telescope. In this test, the most sensitive parameter space predictions for these correlations are obtained. In the final section, we discuss certain technical limitations and potential non-linear relationships of these correlations, that is, the non-linearity of galaxy formation. In this discussion, we propagate uncertainty from lower-redshift observations of individual galaxies to explore ALP dark matter correlations in mock observations of the romanic space telescope. In this test, the predicted sensitivity of the romanic space telescope to these correlations is observed to successfully hold at lower-redshifts, and not least, we propose that ALP dark matter correlations in mock observations of romanic space telescope are a fruitful way to study ALP dark matter. In other words, we propose that ALP dark matter correlations in romanic space telescope data holds considerable potential and in particular, we propose that ALP dark matter correlations in romanic space telescope data may soon serve as a valuable tool to study and explore the complex and deep field phenomenon of cosmic ALP

Our three-dimensional simulations reveal novel mechanisms of non-equilibrium state preservation, which can be exploited for high-capacity, error-correction memory systems. These non-equilibrium states, achieved by rapid quench rates, remain stable even with slow scale changes. Notably, we found that using a broad spectrum of force scales enables memory retention, using only non-equilibrium jammed states. These findings emerge from an analysis of the entropy basis of the solidification transition and the geometrical structure of the jamming phase. Our study provides a new approach to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics and proposes a new approach to self-organization in the absence of thermal fluctuations. Importantly, it lays the groundwork for a new class of high-capacity, fault-tolerant memory storage technologies. Developing robots with skilled arms that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex issue. In response, researchers turn to data-driven approaches involving extensive training on vast simulated datasets. Although such datasets are valuable, they often feature unrealistic input/output conditions due to differences between simulation and real-world settings. As a result, robots may struggle to apply lesson-learned in simulated environments to real-world tasks. To overcome this challenge, we created a massive dataset consisting of over 34,000 high-quality grasp poses on a substantial set of common household objects. In comparison to previous datasets, our collection, named DexGraspNet, offers significantly more diverse objects, diverse poses, and a broader range of difficulties. Furthermore, we employed sophisticated methods to ensure the accuracy of object modeling and grasping in DexGraspNet. Through cross-domain learning using DexGraspNet, our approach significantly improves grasping success rates on a robotic platform transitioning from a realistic game engine to real-world applications. Moreover, combined with domain-adaptive reinforcement learning, training time is greatly reduced and grasping success rates are further elevated to over 96%. The dataset and accompanying project can be accessed at https://github.com/UTIEE/DexGraspNet. A video showcasing the results can be viewed at https://utieee.github.io/DexGraspNet.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a low-rank nonconvex sparsity-based method that distinguishes golden-angle sampled data from phase data. This technique exploits temporal low-rankness, nonconvex l1-f0-sparse subspace and phase data sparsity to reconstruct detailed low-rank temporal bases, separating phase data into spatially varying phase and residual data with detailed low-rank temporal bases for improved reconstruction. Numerical simulations and experimental results show the superiority of the new technique compared with prior approaches. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous channel pruning methods that solely focus on preserving the overall output, InDistill leverages the channel-wise importance of inputs and outputs to capture the key contributions of the teacher model. By setting crucial weight channels in the teacher to allow normal information flow, we enable it to convey valuable knowledge to the student, surpassing the limitations of traditional distillation and pruning alone. Theoretical justification reveals that our method exploits correlations among compact teacher model outputs to mimic full capacity outputs, ensuring the student can accurately replicate the teacher's behavior. Thorough experimentation across multiple datasets affirms the efficacy of our approach, outperforming state-of-the-art model compression techniques. The implementation of InDistill is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/dmkm/IndentifyDistill. Additionally, our compression models can be demonstrated on https://compressedml-with.github.io/. Moreover, we release our own dataset, named CustomML, at https://customml-dmkm.github.io/. Lastly, our research paper detailing InDistill can be found at https://arxiv.org/.

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising threats of degradation and declining productivity. One notable aspect of these ecosystems is the spontaneous formation of plant patterns that can visually appeal, such as the striped arrangements found in many temperate grasslands. Research has demonstrated that these patterns are the result of animal activity, specifically how grazing animals select feeding grounds and diffuse across the landscape. Previous mathematical models examining this pattern formation focus on individual animal behavior, whereas this research aims to expand our understanding by studying the collective movements of grazing animals and how their actions influence the spatial distribution of vegetation. Employing partial differential equations to represent population dynamics, this study reveals that the vegetation spatial pattern is directly correlated with grazing intensity, while their evolution over time is influenced by animals' responsive behavior. Furthermore, this study establishes that born-allocation strategies result in uniform vegetation patterns, whereas death-allocation leads to pattern diversity. Through numerical analysis via ordinary differential equations, this study confirms that the patterns formed are largely independent of the details surrounding birth and death processes, thereby solidifying the role of animal collective behavior in generating distinct plant patterns that can contribute to our understanding of these patterns in natural ecosystems. Moreover, this study provides a mathematical explanation for a phenomenon previously observed in a semi-arid region of Mexico, demonstrating how mathematical models can inform our knowledge of natural processes. We compare mathematical predictions with measured data from the Coparros sector of Mexico. We conclude that our model effectively captures the predicted patterns and demonstrates a satisfactory correlation with real-life data. We propose the application of our model to other dry regions to analyze their dynamics. We conclude that mathematical models can facilitate a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between animal and plant populations in natural ecosystems. We mathematically model how these grazing animals flow through the landscape and how their behavior influences this dynamics. We find that born-allocation results in uniform vegetation patterns, whereas death-allocation leads to diverse patterns. We analyze this dynamics using phase portraits and understand that born-allocation results in uniform, first-order transitions, and homogenous landscapes, whereas death-allocation leads to various transitions and diverse patterns. We discover that, in the case of Mexicaltzingo, the landscape was in a stable equilibrium state. We propose the mathematical modeling of other dry regions to uncover their dynamics. We conclude that mathematical models can facilitate a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between animal and plant populations in natural ecosystems. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively minor number of inferences based on fake data, an issue first documented in 2006 for static scenarios. CountSketch sketches are susceptible to similar manipulated results in sequential settings due to their scalable nature. CountSketch is often used for estimating "approximate" values, but relying solely on the classic estimator can lead to substantial inaccuracies when the data contains patterns or the sketch size isn't substantial in comparison to the data's dimensionality. We've developed two more reliable estimators for CountSketch by analyzing the generative process behind each sketch entry and by using maximum likelihood methods to model dependencies between sketch entries. In our study, generating CountSketch sketches via the original method and then analyzing them with two novel estimators showed improved results in comparison to the classic CountSketch estimator in both static and sequential scenarios. We've also designed CountSketch-specific attacks that force these alternative estimators to provide inaccurate results, thereby highlighting the similar safety issues of dependent sketch designs. On the other hand, generating adversarial examples for CountSketch requires a level of sophistication that parallels or surpasses the capabilities of machine learning and doesn't necessarily work across all dependent sketch designs. As such, CountSketch poses unique challenges in terms of dependency between sketch entries, forcing the creation of sophisticated adversarial examples dependent on multiple sketch entries, and necessitating novel safety assessments for dependent sketch designs that aren't widespread even in the context of CountSketch. Depending on the specific application, generating adversarial examples for CountSketch may require considerable computational resources. In general, adversarial counting tasks turn out to be particularly demanding, requiring precise modifications to input vectors of very high dimension, essentially equivalent to solving optimization problems with numerous constraints. Nonetheless, adapting CountSketch to tasks involving only a few essential dimensions makes it far more resistant to adversarial manipulation. In such circumstances, adversarial counting tasks become much more feasible with the aid of CountSketch, relying as it does on the classic estimator and thus being largely oblivious to dependency between sketch entries, and requiring only very simple optimization, typically sufficient for tasks involving a few essential dimensions. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. Building upon this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values. It is worth noting that this proposed quantum calculus has a compact structure, featuring fewer fundamental components compared to other approaches in the field. The proposed calculus is then utilized to describe the execution of quantum algorithms, with the typing and sematic representations examined in detail for a few exemplary examples. Furthermore, we present a relatively simple set of typing rules, which formsulates a quantum lambda calculus with conclusions, and provide its corresponding categorical interpretation based on the concept of copulas. Ultimately, we discuss these formulations, identify their similarities and differences, and discuss their potential applications, drawbacks, and the avenues for further research. Additionally, we make the relevant development tools available online, including the development of the qrc package on Quipper.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial anisotropic geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. The underlying causes of these similarities and $v_3$'s insensitivity to centrality were further explored. 

In the context of Au+Au collisions, we compared simulated $v_2$ and $v_3$ with PHENIX and STAR measurements, ultimately finding agreement after applying correction factors to our simulations for particle loss. A separate investigation into Cu+Cu collision data found $v_3$ to be in line with PHENIX measurements, while $v_2$ required minimal correction. Derived initial anisotropic geometries displayed comparable characteristics between Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, allowing us to deduce initial anisotropic geometry and flow in both systems. Our findings may provide a basis for additional comparisons with other experimental results in the future.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined from a probabilistic perspective. Unlike traditional interpretations, this work views Kendall's tau as a ratio of probabilities that account for specific ordering among random variables in a sample of data. Because Kendall's tau naturally arises from examining pairs of observations, it is associated with a hierarchical probability distribution that simplifies to a manageable form. By focusing on this probability distribution, researchers can create Bayesian estimators for its parameters, and consequently, for Kendall's tau. Building upon this foundation, novel statistical methods and their performance are evaluated across a range of simulated and real-world datasets. Interestingly, the analysis reveals that the newly proposed statistics exhibit similar properties to those of traditional p-values, yet exhibit different distributional behaviors. Furthermore, the application of these statistical methods to a real-world dataset offers encouraging results, specifically in understanding the relationship between variables representing the number of symptoms and the dosage of medication in patients with schizophrenia. Interestingly, the study finds that the therapeutic effect of certain medications is not significantly influenced by the presence of symptoms when their difference matters, as indicated by the statistical methods and parameters. Nonetheless, the study finds a non-zero correlation between symptoms and the therapeutic effect of certain medications as measured by Kendall's tau. To facilitate further research, the associated software and datasets have been made publicly available. Nevertheless, the study suggests that the use of hierarchical probability distributions could facilitate novel statistical insights when applied to time-series data of unusual statistical phenomena, such as the phenomena observed in schizophrenia research. This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images. The associated software can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/abdosi/EOE. Our paper primarily targets researchers familiar with topological data analysis but inexperienced in multi-variable spaces. We provide a concise review of the relevant methods and prioritize clear, concrete explanations and implementations to facilitate their applications. We also discuss ongoing efforts to enhance the Euler characteristic for refined topological analysis in high-dimensional spaces. These efforts include techniques like persistent homology and the spark analysis, which we briefly introduce. Our main concern, however, is the application of a recent method, also known as exact optimal extrema, to compute the Euler characteristic in multi-variable spaces. We explore its computational feasibility in high-dimensional spaces and discuss its applications in medical imaging, particularly in eye disease detection. The main contributions of our paper are applications of the Euler characteristic in multi-variable spaces, an introduction to the eoe package for computational purposes, and a novel medical imaging application for detecting eye diseases, including diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma, based on multi-variable topological analysis. As an extension of our work, we provide online resources with more applications and a better understanding of the eoe package. The associated DOI for the eoe package is [30584814]. Our paper reports significant results in a controlled study involving 150 patients, demonstrating the efficacy of the method. Our study reveals that the topological analysis has reached state-of-the-art performance in identifying diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma using a single predictor. Furthermore, we achieved impressive multi-variable classification performance of 93% for diabetic retinopathy, 90% for primary glaucoma, and 87% for primary open-angle glaucoma. These figures represent the highest known accuracies for three-way classification among methods that only use a single predictor. Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's equations with a Type II predation response, also incorporating a strong Allee effect in the prey population. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the long-term stability of all species coexistence, and for the extinction of either the prey or predator population in this nonlinear system. We further identify specific parameter relationships that distinguish between unique and unstable saddle point equilibria, and plot corresponding parameter space for a particular parameter pair, verifying our results through numerical calculations and supporting our findings with bifurcation analysis. We graphically represent the parameter regimes that give rise to periodic solutions, demonstrating how the Allee effect contributes to a global predator-prey spectrum that includes extinction, coexistence, and instability. Moreover, our study shows that for a small parameter measurement, the system tends toward a stable limit cycle, characterized by oscillating prey and predator populations. Interestingly, our analysis yields a specific condition under which the predator population experiences extinction. We conclude that for a Type II predation response without the Allee effect, these unique dynamical patterns are no longer observed, and the prey population rapidly declines to zero. Our work thus broadens the understanding of the nonlinear Holling-Tanner dynamics, and their dependence on the Allee effect, highlighting novel scenarios of species coexistence, extinction, and stable limit cycles in predator-prey models. We believe that our results will inspire further theoretical predictions in the study of predator-prey dynamics. Furthermore, our analysis may contribute to a more accurate estimation of demographic parameters in the context of invasive species, and may inspire the development of more effective biological control methods against predators, while warning against the introduction of non-native species for conservation purposes. Finally, our work paves the way for possible applications in disease dynamics, and may facilitate a deeper understanding of the interplay between Allee effects, mutational responses, and limit cycles in diseased and predator-prey models. In the context of environmental sustainability, our analysis raises important questions about the long-term survival of species and the necessity of preserving pristine ecosystems. Ultimately, our results emphasize the significant impact of nonlinear Holling-Tanner dynamics, and the distinct role of the Allee effect, in producing unique dynamical patterns that may not arise in linear predator-prey models. The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research initially conducted by Santos, continued by Boland and Anstreicher, and most recently by Aihan, Biro, Sun, and Sun, demonstrated the impossibility of certain, respectively more sophisticated, linear programming approaches. This paper contributes to the line of research initiated by Santos, showcasing the failure of even the most advanced, polynomial-time linear programming methods in facilitating convergence within n - d iterations. We achieve this outcome by presenting specific n-dimensional polytopes possessing distinct properties: each vertex consists of a single affine function, a single linear equality constraint, and a subset of inequalities derived from this linear constraint. We further propose an efficient algorithm for confirming non-convergence of an n-dimensional linear programming problem in at most n - d iterations, which may have implications in facilitating comparisons between various, high-performance linear programming methods. This standalone algorithm is also integrated into our previously published, polynomial-time, parallel linear programming framework, thereby enabling the detection of non-convergence in parallel, while preserving the online, combinatorial nature required for facilitating efficient iterations and distributed implementation of the approach in question. We establish that our detection method is capable of guaranteeing a bound of O(n d) iterations for confirming non-convergence of an n-dimensional linear programming problem. We establish that our detection method in fact yields an optimal, linear time complexity of O(n^2 d) for confirming non-convergence of an n-dimensional linear programming problem, under the assumption that graph isomorphism problem can be solved in n log d time complexity, under the assumption of Karp's complexity classification. We believe this outcome represents a significant achievement in providing a time-efficient, verification mechanism for confirming non-convergence of an n-dimensional linear programming problem. Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for teaching an autonomous vehicle to maneuver through a highway using reinforcement learning. There are two major hurdles that must be overcome. Firstly, there is the challenge of providing sufficient data for the purpose of training, particularly due to the need for large amounts of pseudo-annotated data in order to fine-tune the autonomous vehicle's observations. Secondly, there is the challenge of teaching the autonomous vehicle to accurately forecast the actions of surrounding vehicles and pedestrians around it, which is essentially an inverse problem that is both computationally and notionally complex. In this research, we present an advanced autonomous highway driving framework, known as HighwayRL, which not only generates compact, hierarchical observations suitable for deep learning and autonomously navigates highway scenarios but also provides an efficient solution to the problem of local object prediction by simulating interactions between the autonomous vehicle and surrounding vehicles. Our framework uses a novel hierarchical attention network to generate compact observations and an multi-layer perceptron to map these compact observations to actions, thereby enabling highway navigation. Moreover, to forecast the local object states, we have developed a duplicate copy mechanism to store a memory of surrounding vehicles and have integrated an attention network to select relevant information. Our approach, which involves imitation learning, provides a solution to the problem of providing a minimal amount of training data. The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be described as either a Lindblad operator or show signs of non-Markovian behavior. Our investigation focuses on a family of gauge-invariant rate operators, derived from high-frequency expansions of rate operators under continuous monitoring, and compares them to their floquet-engineered counterparts in the weak-driving limit. The results reveal a phase transition in this system, characterized by a Lindbladian phase and a non-Markovian phase, differening in their dynamics and spectra. In the non-Markovian phase, an effective, Floquet-engineered Hamiltonian fails to accurately describe the system's behavior, in contrast to its application within the Lindbladian phase. The application of these findings to a qutrit system, including numerical simulations to verify the existence of all three phases, demonstrates their feasibility. Ultimately, these studies contribute to our understanding of how to generalize the application of both phase diagrams and effective Hamiltonians in isolated systems to their open-systems counterparts. Specifically, we find that for quantities not dependent on phase-space correlations, the high-frequency limit of the open system duplicates the behaviour of its isolated counterpart, as does the application of Floquet engineering to model non-equilibrium steady states in driven open systems. However, this is contrary for measures which do rely on phase-space correlations, where the outcome differs significantly, as illustrated through the difference in behaviour observed between the Lindbladian phase and the non-Markovian phase. The potential exists for further exploration of the correlation structure in these systems through numerical investigation. In particular, we observe the induction of coherences in systems naturally possessing only classical states as a defining characteristic of the non-Markovian phase in this context. Conversely, we observe the disappearance of these coherences in the Lindbladian and collinear phases, as might be expected from consideration of these systems in equilibrium. Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 2011 data comprising 3.0 inverse femtobarns collected at the LHC's proton-proton collisions at a 7 TeV center-of-mass energy, a measurement of phi_s is presented. Employing two unbiased algorithms that categorize and measure the CP-sensitive charge asymmetry, the value of phi_s is estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.021 +/- 0.007 radians, with the second uncertainty representing systematic contributions. This outcome is in accordance with the Standard Model prediction encompassing two scenarios based on the optimal neural network discriminant usage, with both outcomes consistent with phi_s = 0. This is the first time phi_s has been measured using baseline charge asymmetry techniques. Furthermore, the results from both methods demonstrate sufficient precision to place a new bound of -0.42 < phi_s < +0.42 at the 68% confidence level on the strong phase delta_mss, which satisfies the unitarity circle constraint. Considering also the usually larger contribution from the weak phase delta_c, this yields -0.753 < phi_s < +0.749. These experimental findings are in agreement with the anticipated range of phi_s = -0.071 +/- 0.102 radians as calculated using the standard model. Given its elevated statistics and enhanced precision, this experiment represents a breakthrough in determining phi_s using data from meson decays. The newly established experimental bounds are in accordance with the predicted range of phi_s based using LHCb's measurements of beta_s, the decay width of the Bs state, and its relative abundance to the B state. The discovered value of phi_s is deemed to be the most precise and precise measurement to date. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph nodes) in relation to specific properties (edges) using the standard graph structure. However, this approach has limitations, as it assumes a static graph, which may not be the case for all machine learning tasks. In contrast, we address the more general problem of attribute-based explanation by leveraging a flexible, expandable graph framework, which allows us to adapt to tasks where the graph changes, such as in the case of image classification. Our proposed method provides accurate and comprehensive attribute-based explanations, outperforming existing baselines in accuracy and visual plausibility, as evidenced by our experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into our approach, highlighting its advantages over comparative methods. Our source code and datasets are publicly available.
