Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the naming game with migrating entities reveals how migration affects language development. (i) In scenarios where all agents are mobile, a collective phenomenon emerges that promotes language homogenization. This effect is highly consistent and observable across various agent densities and mobility levels. This led to the hypothesis that mobile agents are capable of accelerating the language convergence process. (ii) However, when only a fraction of agents can move, their migration has an unexpected effect. Mobile agents facilitate language fragmentation by dispersing monolingual groups throughout the population, whereas stationary agents have a homogenizing effect. (iii) In instances where agents choose whether to migrate based on language usage, a mechanism promoting the language fragmentation of large populations into distinct, mutually incomprehensible languages is observed. This process relies on low to moderate mobility levels and dense agent distributions. Furthermore, our analysis using an ordinary differential equation model indicates that individual migration decisions based on language usage can lead to the fragmentation of languages, both in theoretical populations and in realistic models. These findings demonstrate that migration is a crucial factor in shaping language and sheds new light on this complex phenomenon, ultimately explaining how languages may split and converge over time. These results were verified using Monte Carlo simulations in open-source Python code, which is available for further research. This allows for the investigation of how population size, mobility levels, and individual migration decisions based on language influence the evolution of languages into separate, mutually incomprehensible languages or a converged, single language. Importantly, our study highlights that both migration and language use are crucial in determining language development. By combining these two factors, it becomes possible to explain how languages may split and converge over time, leading to more accurate predictions regarding language evolution. PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal convergence when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have investigated how PINNs train under a momentum-based stochastic gradient descent. Our findings indicate that incorporating momentum substantially diminishes the impact of spectral bias, leading to better convergence. Additionally, we discovered that using the Adam optimizer not only reduces spectral bias but also accelerates convergence. Our numerical experiments further demonstrate that wide-enough networks using stochastic gradient descent can still converge to optimal solutions, even when the target function contains high-frequency features, highlighting the importance of network width in achieving convergence. Finally, our adapted nnewt framework allows for efficient numerical integration to validate our findings, providing an improved tool for solving ordinary differential equations and partial differential equations. Our work lays the groundwork for further exploration of optimization techniques to alleviate spectral biases in PINNs. Our source code is available for review at https://github.com/kemans/nnewt.

Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly due to the waves being coupled and the non-smooth damping coefficient, specifically that it loses its rapid exponential stability and instead experiences a slowing decay at a rate no better than $t^{-\frac{1}{12}}$. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs incur significant expenses in real-world settings, while a lack of interpretability makes it difficult to understand and improve intricate decision-making processes. In an effort to reduce sample costs, we focus on a fundamental challenge: building flexible models for non-Markovian policies in offline RL settings. We present a novel framework called Markov Aggregation (MarkoAgg) that aims to lower the sample cost by enabling more general policy representations. Through a kernel-based approach, MarkoAgg aggregates a large collection of Markov decision processes into a single, flexible distribution over trajectories, allowing us to compute optimal actions using only the aggregated distribution. We propose a deep MarkoAgg model that estimates the parameterizing distribution of the two-time deep MDP, resulting in the state-dependent policy (SDP) and the policy-dependent state (PDS) models. We conduct rigorous experiments that reveal the superiority of MarkoAgg over existing state-of-the-art approaches, while our analysis demonstrates that MarkoAgg offers novel transparency and expressiveness aspects. Furthermore, we extend MarkoAgg to tackle the challenges of continuous action spaces, yielding the corresponding continuous MarkoAgg model. We evaluate the continuous MarkoAgg model on several hard-exploration RL tasks and find that it surpasses prior work in achieving stability and transparency. We visually illustrate the learned kernels of MarkoAgg in our supplementary material, showcasing its potential for interpretability. Overall, our proposed continuous MarkoAgg model presents an innovative approach to offline RL, offering promising avenues for transparent and efficient deep RL. The code for our methods is available at https://github.com/ziplab/continuous-markoagg. MarkoAgg has the potential to lower interaction costs in offline RL, an area that warrants further research. We hope that our contributions inspire future work in this domain. In particular, one potential future research direction is to extend continuous MarkoAgg to online RL settings to reduce the time complexity. An alternative research direction is to investigate how MarkoAgg can be used as a tool for debugging and identifying issues in pre-trained RL agents. Lastly, one future research direction is to extend the proposed continuous MarkoAgg model using techniques from meta-learning to reduce the required interactions for the target task. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between the resonators that allows us to generate a nonreciprocal transmission relationship between the resonators. Notably, we've demonstrated that the degree of nonreciprocal transmission can be precisely controlled by adjusting the amount of squeezed light generated. Our strategy for optical nonreciprocity doesn't rely on a balance of coupling, does enhance the nonreciprocal transmission efficiency, and is compatible with a wide range of physical mechanisms for squeezing. We successfully implemented this method in an actual GaAs-based three-resonator system, demonstrating a nearly complete nonreciprocal transmission efficiency with less than 1 mW of pump power. The integration of our technique could greatly enhance the performance and reliability of optical communication systems, traffic management in optical data centers and the production of optical certifiers. Furthermore, we've shown that the application of squeezed light can significantly reduce losses in optical circuits where losses exceed 10 dB. Notably, we've successfully applied this method to a complex optical circuit that was previously thought to be nonfunctional. The remarkable capabilities of our all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity and its potential for developing loss-optical circuits. Moreover, we've shown that the application of squeezed light can precisely control the flow of light in complex optical systems and make feasible optical circuits that were previously considered nonfunctional.

A new category called BiHom/BiQuasi-Yang-Baxter modules has been formally defined and its related systems and equations such as BiHom/Yang-Baxter and BiQuasi/Yang-Baxter have been explicitly defined within it. This development constitutes the first comprehensive study of its module-like objects, which in turn enables an examination of associated BiHom/Yang-Baxter modules and their role in solving the BiHom/double curved Rota-Baxter system, a system previously unsolved. Using the BiHom/Yang-Baxter module as a guiding principle, a new algebraic structure - BiHom/shapiro-finite Yang-Baxter module - is introduced and its properties explored. This new structure serves as an extension to BiHom/Yang-Baxter modules and sheds new light on solving BiHom/double curved Rota-Baxter systems. Furthermore, BiHom/shapiro-finite Yang-Baxter modules provide a new algebraic perspective on module-like objects for BiHom/Yang-Baxter systems and offer significant advancements in solving the BiHom/double curved Rota-Baxter system. This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its modified Friedmann equation is analogous to that of the APS LQC model. Notably, the model's critical matter density at the bounce point is a quarter of the original APS LQC model's, with the critical density $\rho_{cL}$ equalling $\frac{\rho_c}{4}$. This discovery implies that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than previously thought and also make detection more feasible due to a lower critical density. Interestingly, the model's behavior in terms of momentum (in terms of Hamiltonian constraints) mirrors that of the previously proposed models. Following modification to tackle the singularities in the Hamiltonian, this research finds that both inflation and contraction occur within bounded energy ranges. Moreover, restoring the correct Hamiltonian dynamics results in a more substantial value for the maximum momentum than found in the comparable APS LQC model. It's also found that curvature scale $A$ dictates whether there will be inflation in this model: a $A > 1$ suggests an accelerating universe, whereas $A < 1$ indicates deceleration. Lastly, similar to other LQC models, this setup offers hope for an inflationary origin to our universe's observed homogeneity and homoplastic properties. To achieve this, the universe would need to undergo inflation at a similar energy scale to what was previously thought necessary in the APS LQC model, that is with $H \approx 10^{14}$ GeV. Nonetheless, the discovery that quantum gravity effects will manifest earlier than anticipated, along with a lower critical density, presents an increasingly attractive possibility for an inflationary cosmology arising from LQC, where the onset of these effects during the very early universe could possibly explain observed homogeneity and homoplastic properties. However, the model is incapable of explaining why this universe is asymptotically flat; a flat universe in this model is not a prediction, but rather an requirement for a comparable analysis as seen with similar models. To further understand this, a more in-depth analysis of an anisotropic spatially closed LFCQ model is recommended to see if a model predicting an isotropic universe can be formulated. 

This research provides a novel contribution to the realm of LFCQ models, opening up the possibility for a broader range of research into these models, encompassing analyses of new setups, scenarios, and cases, expanding our understanding of modified Hamiltonian dynamics and its applications.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods, particularly Monte Carlo dropout and Bayesian neural networks, to track object detection probabilities. However, applying these methods requires substantial computational resources or detailed knowledge of the network's probabilistic properties, which is usually impractical. This paper presents an efficient technique for generating accurate uncertainty scores in minimal computational time by combining dropout with a straightforward, low-cost variational method. Experimental evaluations on popular computer vision datasets demonstrate the proposed method's capability to achieve accurate object detection uncertainty scores in real-time. The proposed method requires minimal modifications to the network code and is suitable for complex systems like robotic networks. Furthermore, the method can easily accommodate sophisticated architectures, such as ResNet, to provide reliable uncertainty scores for ambiguous inputs. The results also demonstrate that accurate object detection relies heavily on properly estimating the probabilities of background classes. Additionally, the method's success paves the way for the development of reliable autonomous systems. The proposed method's source code is available for review. 

Keywords: uncertainty estimation, probabilistic object detection, deep neural networks, minimal computational cost.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems.
The traffic4cast competition pushed the limits of short-term traffic prediction, leveraging high-resolution traffic volume and speed data, available in five-minute intervals. 
To adapt to new cities, as the 2021 challenge demanded, a more effective approach is suggested: predicting local sections rather than a city's entire grid.
By breaking down test data into smaller overlapping segments at test time, prediction accuracy and stability improve due to parallel processing of traffic patterns within these frames.
Using convolutional neural networks (CNNs), as in real-time traffic prediction, yields suboptimal results due to difficulty in learning the larger grid's overall state.
A simple transformer architecture is proposed to aggregate predictions from individual patches, as well as a secondary network to combine features from patch-level transformers.
The method outperforms previous competition submissions, as demonstrated by this paper's results. 
To facilitate replication, the code and pre-trained models are made publicly available.

We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical interactions that can be quickly calculated. We also broadened the scope of Squier's theorem to fit our research framework, which led us to the discovery that convergent rewriting systems lead to coherence in Gray categories. To prove this, we established a connection between Gray categories and tricategories, allowing us to apply existing proof structures from the literature. Our study culminates in a key result: any congruence generated by a rewriting system on Gray categories is also derived from the corresponding tricategorical coherence. This result is a significant breakthrough in understanding the relationship between Gray categories and tricategories. Interestingly, our approach shows that the notion of weak structures arises naturally from the presence of commutative monoidal or symmetric structures. Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We compared this method with other recent deep learning techniques in two datasets: the public HarP dataset and an in-house epilepsy dataset, HCUnicamp. Despite surpassing other methods in terms of Dice score, our approach as well as other tested methods failed to completely avoid false positives in resection regions when applied to epilepsy patients, indicating room for further improvement. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate proton radiation at low Earth orbit by simulating the interaction between cosmic ray particles and the Earth's atmosphere, followed by transportation in the magnetosphere. This includes modeling particle generation, dispersion, and loss processes. The resulting radiation levels are validated through comparisons with data from the PAMELA experiment at various low Earth orbit altitudes. Furthermore, the proposed radiation belt dynamics is extended to consider its temporal variations by incorporating the influence of seasonal variations in the Earth's atmospheric density, as well as an examination of transient effects triggered by solar storms. The study finds significant transients in radiation levels influenced by solar storms, yielding increases of up to double or more compared to normal conditions. These results have crucial implications for reducing uncertainties in radiation protection design for space vehicles and spacecraft. Moreover, our simulations show that radiation reconstruction through inversion of space radiation data can successfully recover the radiation contribution from solar storms, but fails to do so for seasonal variations or other transients. This highlights the necessity of developing new techniques for reconstruction that can account for non-stationary processes in radiation dynamics. The proposed radiation reconstruction framework, an essential tool for designing space radiation protection systems, requires integration with current radiation data campaigns to enhance our understanding of radiation dynamics. The study suggests a novel approach for reconstruction which utilizes a Bayesian neural network to accurately predict radiation levels and their spatial distribution. The study's findings on radiation predictions are further validated through applications to other low Earth orbit missions such as PAMELA and TRACER, as well as other spatial locations, demonstrating the technique's versatility. A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel framework for addressing expressivity in DNNs via 
certificate-based lower bounds on the error rate. This framework achieves this 
by categorizing a DNN's representational capabilities using polynomial equations 
and determining its error bounds based on the distance between its output and the 
true labels, thus paving the way for more effective generalization 
characterizations. Additionally, our approach enhances existing inferential 
expressivity bounds that focus solely on classification errors, allowing for 
polynomial equation representation that captures both classification and 
regression errors. This framework also facilitates the development of tailored 
network architectures that maximize a particular expressivity metric, as 
demonstrated through modifications made to well-established networks like ResNet and 
Inception, resulting in significant improvements in their generalization 
performance. Lastly, our approach's potential for handling complex representational 
patterns is explored through the examination of polynomial equation-based 
expressivity in overparameterized, sufficiently complex networks. Using random 
 Fourier and perturbation-based techniques, our research shows that this 
framework enables characterization of representational capabilities of very large 
networks, breaking the traditional correlation between expressivity and training 
time. This breakthrough opens the door for further investigation into how 
polynomial equation-based expressivity can be utilized to inform both the 
architecture and optimization of future deep neural networks. The source code 
associated with this research is available at https://github.com/dmvgao/expressivity.

performance of this Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the Alternating Least Squares method to solve matrix completion tasks.
Furthermore, we apply the Iteratively Re-Weighted Least Squares algorithm and
investigate how different noise-based approaches function in both artificial and
real datasets. Experimental findings show that the Huber mechanism meets the

better robustness to outliers compared to other noise-based methods. Since
alternating optimization is a free implementation of the ALS algorithm, we
recommend utilizing this method in practical applications to solve matrix
completion tasks. As an alternative, we suggest utilizing the iterative
least squares method, which is a more robust alternative to gradient-based

Research into highly eccentric gas giant planets around low-mass stars is crucial 
to understanding the formation of giant planets early in a star's lifetime and 
to determining if they can have active lives in the universe's longest existing 
stars. Current models of planet formation suggest these stars can have compact 
systems containing planets of smaller mass. However, there is a lack of reliable 
data on the average mass of planets they can have. Our study looked at data from 
transit missions, including TESS and Gaia, for 132 stars with a mass no bigger than 
a third of the sun's mass, over a period when these planets would reflect more 
intensely than their host stars, to identify and analyze any discovered planets. 
We applied our own methods to analyze the data, which allowed us to identify seven 
planets in total, six of which were found using TESS data. These planets were 
estimated to have a minimum mass of 0.4 and 2.8 times that of the earth respectively. 
Our research suggests these planets could have formed within a disc that had 
structures that prevented it from being uniform, according to theoretical 
planet-formation studies. These planets were also found to have longer orbits in 
proportion to their size, which could be a result of them forming at a time when 
their host stars were younger, providing further evidence that these planets do 
exist and could have active lives in the universe's longest existing stars.

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined arrangement. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, which revolves around determining the most clicks required to solve any given configuration of lights in a grid-based graph. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods when applied to a range of test images. Furthermore, the feasibility and efficacy of this approach are also verified through several applications, including 3D shape reconstruction from a single or multiple images, image segmentation assisted by texture analysis, and 3D cardiac mesh reconstruction from MRI images. Detailed effects and observations are discussed in the appendix. The proposed technique is implemented in a publicly available code on GitHub. A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties that contribute to a variety of technological applications. Topological phonons, encompassing nodal rings, lines, and points, are found in different oxide perovskite systems, encompassing structural forms (tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral), compounds (BaTiO3, PbTiO3, SrTiO3), and external influences (photoexcitation, strain, temperature). Notably, tetragonal perovskite compounds stabilized through photoexcitation exhibit all topological phonon types simultaneously, whereas thermal stabilization primarily supports a limited set of topological phonon states. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential to regulate topological phonon states through photoinduced carrier concentrations without accompanying structural transformations, suggesting that light manipulation may lead to transitions between states without altering the phase of the system. We propose perovskite oxides as a versatile experimental platform to investigate topological phonons and manipulate them with the aid of light. Since nodal lines and rings of phonons can arise in phases that exhibit no topological electrons (as observed in SrTiO3 and PbTiO3), light-induced transitions between these phonon configurations hold the potential to facilitate phase transitions in non-topological insulators. Conversely, we highlight that nodal planes, which are typically investigated in the strong spin-orbit coupling regime of topological phonons, are unlikely to be realized in perovskite oxides due to less pronounced spin-orbit coupling. Spin-orbit coupling in these materials is predominantly induced by octahedral angle deformations, which are generally minimized in perovskite structures. Consequently, we demonstrate that, in the strong spin-orbit coupling regime typically investigated in two-dimensional materials, topological phonons exhibiting nodal planes do not form in perovskite insulators. However, we propose that light-induced transitions between these phonon configurations hold the potential to facilitate phase transitions in non-topological insulators, which may host topological electrons under external influences. We estimate that a moderate photoexcitation of about 10% can induce a topological insulating phase in tetragonal perovskite compounds. Consequently, we predict that light-induced transitions among these phonon configurations hold the potential to facilitate phase transitions in non-topological insulators, which may host topological electrons under external influences. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle distance-based outlier detection effectively, given the growing availability of powerful computational environments. Current implementations in R lack efficiency and often incorporate complex architectures, making them difficult to distribute for parallel computing on modern hardware. In response, we developed a novel parallel computing framework for distance-based outlier detection and implemented it in C++ as PbOD, which achieves a substantial performance improvement over existing R libraries while facilitating scalable parallel computations on modern GPUs or multiple cores, thereby accelerating analysis by at least one order of magnitude. Comparisons with R libraries reveal that PbOD significantly outperforms these tools, offering a scalable solution that can leverage the capabilities of modern computing hardware. The open-source C++ code and comprehensive Python interface make PbOD a versatile tool suitable for various data analysis tasks. You can access the code at https://github.com/complexity-of-motion/pbod/. Our experimental results examine the performance of PbOD on various machine learning datasets, considering the impact of parallel processing on accuracy in different distance metrics. These benchmarks measure the speed and efficiency of PbOD on modern hardware, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world data analysis. The supplementary material at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.03525 provides an in-depth comparison with existing R libraries, detailing both the efficiency gains achieved by PbOD and any potential discrepancies in outlier detection accuracy when comparing PbOD to popular open-source R libraries. Our results show that PbOD's implementation in C++ significantly enhances the analysis speed while offering a comparable outlier detection accuracy, offering a valuable replacement for existing tools in R. Our prediction is that PbOD's efficient parallel computing framework will also appeal to programmers outside the Java environment. Our results further reveal that PbOD's effective rescaling allows the tool to adapt seamlessly to the analysis of data involving various types and scales, making it entirely suitable for large-scale applications involving heterogeneous data in metric spaces. Our final observation is that PbOD's computational efficiency has considerable implications for real-time applications in fields like the monitoring of complex networks and the analysis of event sequences, providing an essential advance towards making these tools more scalable and applicable in the context of time-series analysis. As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is based on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link prediction, we delve into fair link classification as part of the graph representation learning task. Through comprehensive evaluations, we showcase the effectiveness of our neighborhood fairness framework across multiple graph machine learning tasks and observe that fairness achieved through node-based approaches consistently benefits downstream task performance. Furthermore, we observe that our framework's design considers inherent relationships between tasks and seeks to enhance generalizability, a characteristic that remains underexplored in the fair learning realm. All implementation details can be found on the https://github.com/tomafar/Neighborhood-Fairness repository. 
This research introduces the concept of neighborhood fairness and a associated framework that aims to achieve it, combining compliance with data constraints to ensure fairness is achieved. To validate its effectiveness, we apply the framework to multiple graph machine learning tasks, including fair link classification, which holds significance as a fundamental component of graph representation learning. Notably, our findings indicate that fairness at the node level, as opposed to global fairness, is relevant in modern graph-based applications, a trend we aim to shed more light on in the discussion section. Moreover, our work explores how fairness impacts the generalizability of graph representation learning, a area of study that remains understudied. Consequently, our research aims to contribute to the understanding of neighborhood fairness and its implications for the more general concept of fairness in graph-based learning systems. 
Ultimately, our hope is that our research, describing various neighborhood fairness paradigms, the challenges they pose, and how they impact different machine learning tasks, as well as our efforts to address them through novel methods, will stimulate future inquiry into the complex and multifaceted concept of fairness in graph representation learning. 
In particular, our work on fair link prediction reveals that advanced GNN models, capable of operating at a graph level, are susceptible to unfairness at the node level, stresses the need for more comprehensive evaluations of their fairness beyond current assessments based on global metrics only.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  To verify the accuracy of these approximations, we analyze the residual errors in the context of well-known limiting cases in chemical kinetics.  Furthermore, we devise a graphical test for assessing the accuracy of approximations and analyze it using the Canne-Wilkinson model for Michaelis-Menten type reactions.  We also compare the computational efficiency of these methods by determining the number of iterations required to achieve canne-like convergence.  Supporting materials, including Flowcharts and graphs, are provided online.  In addition, we discuss possible applications of these approximations to other types of equations.  Furthermore, a public-domain graphing package is recommended for visualizing the behavior of these approximations, and a tentative roadmap is proposed for extending these methods to analyze non-linear equations describing reversible reactions.  Finally, code is supplied online for generating the graphs in this study. Theoretical physicists conduct experiments in final states featuring jets and numerous leptons to investigate a specific hypothesis in which a gluino decomposes into two squarks. These squarks are considered to be virtually present in the form of light mass when their masses are close to the energy range of the LHC. By using the gluino-squark production in association with heavy bosons as a reference point, researchers introduce a new search approach focused on the gluino decay into three quarks involving long-lived gluinos. This new search approach exploits properties of the gluino's disappearance in the form of metamorphosing tracks and takes into account the characteristics of the gluino's out-of-the-ordinary decay length in an algorithmic manner. When applying this new search approach to a dataset of 139 fb^-1 from the LHC's Run 2, researchers conclude that the search offers the most competitive bounds on the gluino's mass at 3.2 TeV when its mass decomposes into quarks without any virtual intermediate states. Furthermore, the search's sensitivity reaches up to a mass of 4.2 TeV when including an unbounded range for the squark's mass. These findings represent discovery levels that have never before been achieved in theoretical models representing a combination of split SUSY scenarios and long-lived gluinos. The search's relevant diffusion properties have been used to set bounds in theoretical models involving the direct decay of the squark into the gluino and a Higgs boson. This new search approach failed to detect a sign of a gluino in a theoretical framework that splits masses in which the squarks' mass is taken as a mass at a midpoint of 1 TeV. Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles are explored, assuming the market participants can see through arbitrage. Initially, the market reaches a stable equilibrium where fundamental and expected values align, but an external shock sets off a rapid increase in prices. This price surge can terminate abruptly, ending the bubble. Additional analysis considers the varied behaviors of multiple arbitrageurs with shifting expectations, revealing that the emergence and persistence of bubbles depend on a mixture of risk-taking and heterogeneous arbitrage. A publicly accessible simulation tool has been created using Python to examine this model and its outcomes in detail. The related work notes include further research pointers on bubbles, AR model, lognormal model, normal model, maximum likelihood estimation, the options market, portfolio selection and continuous-time financial model. Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to produce high-quality CS text, specifically focusing on Hindi-English CS text. An innovative approach is proposed that employs a latent space model to generate innovative words by rearranging existing words. Furthermore, this research outlines a set of rules for creating innovative CS sentences by altering the word order according to functional categorizations. Two models are developed to create new CS sentences: one based on a neural model that identifies innovative words and another utilizing a sequence-to-sequence model that can handle word replacements. Evaluation of word creativity and text coherence demonstrates that the proposed data augmentation methods for CS text are effective. Furthermore, this study examines the potential of the generated data in improving the performance of CS NLP tasks by conducting a search-based optimization experiment that fine-tunes model parameters using data augmentation methods as variables. The results indicate that the proposed methods enhance the performance of CS NLP tasks. For instance, this study reports an improvement from 66.98 to 69.05 in the BLEU score for Hindi-English CS translation, thereby validating the utility of data augmentation methods for CS NLP. The study provides open-source access to the data augmentation code. Moreover, this study contributes novel CS datasets by applying data augmentation methods to both word and sentence levels. Specifically, this study publishes 10,000 new innovative Hindi-English CS sentences produced by deep learning-based methods. Moreover, this study provides 1,440 new CS sentence pairs for a translation task, thereby increasing the total number of existing pairs by 2,000 times. The study also reports innovative CS sentence counts on Twitter, thereby providing valuable insights into the dynamics of innovative CS sentence usage on this platform. The research outcomes offer a ground-breaking approach to generating high-quality CS data, thereby opening up new avenues for research in this area. As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental concept in addressing these challenges is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral units offer enhanced computational advantages. However, mesh integrity relies on the quality of its components. The issue arises when elements take on shapes hindering precise calculations, rendering them unusable. To deliver accurate outcomes, it is crucial to correct such elements' morphology, making the mesh robust. Currently, mesh modification techniques are labor-intensive and often inefficient and, therefore, inefficient. To tackle this problem, this paper presents a new approach to transforming an input mesh into a refined, high-quality version. This study introduces a unified mathematical model for the static power dissipation of CMOS inverter circuits, applicable to different technologies characterized by variable threshold voltages over time. The proposed analysis, built on existing theoretical foundations, offers a comprehensive and generalizable assessment of inverter delay, driven by short-circuit currents, leveraging existing experimental data to derive key parameters. In conjunction with the proposed model, this research tests and compares the impact of different CMOS inverter characteristics on static power consumption and delay using CMOS technologies spanning four decades, attributing delays primarily to RC time constants due to increasing subthreshold current with scaling, and highlights the significance of load capacitance, inverter size, and CMOS technology characteristics. Furthermore, the study derives a practical expression for predicting the delay of deep-submicron CMOS inverters under varying technological settings. Evaluations of the proposed model's accuracy based on metrics such as average absolute and relative error demonstrate satisfactory predictions with an average absolute error below 4% across the technologies studied, and the derived mathematical expressions demonstrate the ability to capture the complex dynamics of CMOS inverter behavior through two key parameters, independent of technology. The study provides further evidence that a particular set of parameters can effectively characterize the trade-offs between power dissipation and processing speed in CMOS technologies. The research contributes a mathematical framework for predicting the static power consumption and delay of CMOS inverter circuits at different technology stages, and explores how these predictions can be utilized for six CMOS technology benchmarking from the ITC'92 benchmark cross-talk dataset. Lastly, the study derives a practical expression for predicting the static power consumption of high-performance CMOS inverter circuits at different technology stages. In summary, this research contributes a versatile and generalizable mathematical framework for assessing the static power consumption and delay of CMOS inverter circuits with variable threshold voltages, and explores the design trade-offs between these performance metrics in deep-submicron CMOS technologies. The research further provides accurate and detailed predictions of CMOS inverter behavior across diverse technology platforms. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The data presented could inform the development of more effective treatments for neurological disorders like visual agnosia and aphasia. The study further highlights the effectiveness of novel computational and behavioral methods in elucidating neural mechanisms, enabling more precise explanations of human disorders and their effects. The current research contributes to ongoing discussions regarding the organization of the ventral temporal cortex, offering insights into this critical region essential for normal visual perception and communication but also vulnerable to damage in neurological disorders. The study's findings also raise important considerations regarding the representation of social agents versus non-agents, raising essential ethical implications and questions regarding the representation of humans versus non-human animals. The study addresses these hypotheses using cutting-edge neuroimaging technologies, behavior experiments, and computational models, promoting dialogue about the representation of social agents versus non-agents in the human brain. The research further promotes dialogue about the representation of humans versus non-human animals at the neurobiological level, encouraging necessary considerations for important ethical implications. The study's findings provide valuable insights into understanding, treating, and preventing disorders such as visual agnosia and aphasia by mapping the complex animacy spectrum in VTC. The research conducted is part of a larger project aiming to advance treatment options for patients struggling with visual and verbal communication disorders. The data presented in the study offers significant implications for other domains within VTC, such as actions, objects, and scenes, suggesting that distinct governing principles may shape these representations and necessitate further investigation. Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) are a notable feature of black hole X-ray transients known as Nova Orlowski. Research into the source Nova Orlowski has revealed the existence of type-C QPOs, typically appearing in low-hard and fuzzy boundary states with distinct QPO characteristics. To gain insights, scientists have collected and analyzed 33 known episodes of state transitions in Nova Orlowski, observed between 2015 and 2017. Each episode was examined with high time-resolution X-ray data from the Fermi/GBM and Insight-HXMT, allowing researchers to detect and analyze transitions, measure the widths of soft X-ray bands, and track variations in light curves. Furthermore, by utilizing an advanced model, they were able to fit joint spectral analyses and measure the frequencies of corona instability, verifying that the source exhibits distinct characteristics in various states. These findings have been published in a study entitled "Observations of corona instability frequencies across different spectral states of Nova Orlowski," showing that the frequency of instability is longest in the low-hard state and shortest in the soft states. Also, an accompanying Corradi et al. study examines the possibility that Novae Orlowski's observed phenomena are due to the movement of a floating post-thermonuclear fusion sheet within an unstable accretion flow. While the studies primarily focus on Nova Orlowski's behavior, they also highlight the importance of analyzing other transients to better understand how the physics of accretion flows, bi-stable flows, and semi-relativistic two-flow vary between sources. Here, we propose a theoretical framework based on bi-stable flows to explain complex observations of luminous low-mass X-ray transients and their associated QPOs. Additionally, our results suggest that the physics of accretion in bi-stable flows is a recurring phenomenon in many X-ray binaries, as demonstrated by our studies in Figures 10, 11, and 12. Here, we predict the existence of specific types of QPOs in several targets, such as MAXI J0911-094, SSTB109, CXOJ164712.2-445240, and NX Orionis Z. Our findings serve as a reminder that a comprehensive understanding of X-ray binary physics requires comprehensive study of all types of low-mass X-ray binaries. Finally, our results indicate that bi-stable flows provide an ideal environment for post-thermonuclear fusion processes to occur, and as such, these phenomena could be more common

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between the actions of individual agents and aims to guide MARL agents toward developing reactive approaches. Three simulated cooperation scenarios confirm our hypothesis that this approach can improve the performance of MARL agents in diverse groups and reduce dependence on explicit communication mechanisms. Moreover, our findings indicate that this method can be utilized effectively in a wide range of empirical studies. Our research implies that utilizing transfer empowerment could lead to more efficient training of MARL agents that are capable of working effectively together. We then derive and illustrate in examples the definitions of homotopy modules and shifted Lie and Lie homotopy algebra structures, as well as the concept of cohomology and cohomology classes. To further develop these Lie 2-algebras, two explicit constructions are provided: the twisted Lie 2-algebra of a 2-term L∞-algebra with a pre-Lie module and the cohomology 2-term L∞-algebra of a differential graded Lie algebra. We also introduce two analogs of integrability conditions for these structures and prove that certain pre-Lie 2-algebras meet these criteria. Finally, three integrable Lie 2-algebras are explicitly described. Specifically, their cohomology Lie 2-algebras are isomorphic to the truncated cohomology of a two-dimensional Lie homotopy algebra derived from a three-dimensional Lie algebra, and two of these are equivalent to the cohomology Lie 2-algebra of the three-dimensional Lie algebra u(3) and the Lie 2-algebra derived from the assosymmetric 3-cohomology Lie algebra of the exterior algebra. In particular, the cohomology Lie 2-algebra of u(3) is integrable in the reduced case (β=γ=0). We also show that the cohomology Lie 2-algebra of the assosymmetric 3-cohomology Lie algebra of the exterior algebra is integrable. We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that are context-dependent for both images. This approach allows our method, known as LoFTR, to effectively find dense matches in low-texture regions where traditional detectors face difficulties. Experiment results on indoor and outdoor datasets demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods with significant margin and excels on visual localization tasks, topping rankings on two prominent benchmarks. Additionally, our method's source code and pre-trained models are freely available.

This research splits the Earth into a grid of polygons to examine the longest annual burning periods across various global regions. Analyzing satellite imagery from the MODIS Terra satellite, it identifies daily fire images and counts to determine the longest consecutive days of burning per region. Evaluating 2000-2011 data, it finds most regions experienced fire seasons lasting under 130 days. Notably, regions like Africa and regions near equatorial latitudes had even shorter season lengths. A new analysis technique, called satellite proximity weighting, is introduced to reduce bias caused by data collection gaps. This method distributes data points based on the proximity of the satellite to the observed location, thereby improving accuracy. Compared to existing estimates, satellite proximity weighting reduces mean error by 58%, thereby providing improved estimates of fire duration. Using this method, it is found that regions like Africa, India, and parts of the equatorial regions had lower Durbin-Singleton error rates. Furthermore, it is observed that regions with longer fire seasons tend to have higher annual fire counts. The analysis further reveals that regions with extended fire seasons are not necessarily experiencing an increase in total fire counts. This finding contradicts prior research linking rising global temperatures to increased fire activity. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a substantial portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated. Specifically, we find that three of the measures exhibit strong positive correlations with each other, while five others display negative correlations with the leading principal component. This outcome implies that these metrics, although distinct, might be viewed as alternative manifestations of the same theoretical concept of morphological complexity. To further validate this hypothesis, we employ a structural equation model and provide an interpretation of the results within the framework of the Complexity Weighted Tree Model. The model's parameters offer insight into the specific morphological aspects that drive variability among the measures in question. Our findings have important implications for linguists working in the field, advising on language engineering projects concerned with words lists, morphological analysis, or parsing – particularly in languages rich in inflectional morphology. The study also sets a foundation for exploring the intricate relationship between morphological and syntactic complexity in future research. The study's code and data are freely accessible for download.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news which typically go live on social media first. There's been minimal research undertaken to explore Twitter's 2015 event data, incorporating tweets from 50 nations. Our study tackles this challenge, providing a real-time event detection framework that leverages social media data. It comprises two main components: an innovative algorithm for detecting events and a clustering methodology. First, the data is processed to extract relevant information based on distinct places and time frames. Secondly, the data is reorganized to group tweets by location and time to detect trending events across different countries. Our analysis also generates maps to represent active and popular events across various regions, including different cities within the same country and across multiple nations. The findings from our study are based on 50+ million annotated tweets spanning 50 nations, covering a period of 1.5 years. Evaluations have been conducted using both human and machine-based metrics to verify the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Building upon this concept, our aim is to develop a practical application that enables users to explore trending events across different countries based on their interests, location, or timeline. The proposed solution provides a dynamic visual representation of these events on an interactive map, which can be customized using various filters. Interestingly, our analysis has revealed that many events have been misclassified over a period of time, including incidents such as those involving Zika and the Olympics. Furthermore, our study has identified trending events on topics including crime, social issues, and natural disasters across different countries. The findings have also revealed real-time trends in countries such as the US, Mexico, India, the UK, and Australia. Most of these events have been categorized under the theme of breaking news, including incidents such as road accidents and fires in rural areas. Furthermore, our study has identified popular events on social media including protests for real social change, the global campaign for the fight against AIDS, the movement for same-sex marriage, the killing of civilians and law enforcement officials, and  the demands for refugee resettlement in different countries. The research demonstrates that Twitter event annotations provide valuable insights into understanding trends in 50 nations. The study has also revealed correlations between the disappearance of events over time and the decrease in their popularity based on user preferences. The findings have further revealed similarities in human classification and ranking of social media events on various topics. The research aims to address the research gap in this area by developing a robust real-time event analysis framework

This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in one subsystem given another's specific measurement. Research has previously established that when Alice and Bob share a Gaussian state, Bob can create Wigner negativity in Alice's system through measurement, if and only if there is a steering influence from Alice's to Bob's system. Specifically, this steering influence causes Bob's measurements to sublinearly transform specific phase-space projections of the shared Gaussian state. This sublinearity phenomenon underlies all instances of remote Wigner negativity and we illustrate its connection to different nonclassical correlations in our research. Furthermore, our results indicate that when multiple copies of a Gaussian state are available, Bob can determine if the state is pure and unentangled with Alice, thanks to the possibility of remotely generating Wigner negativity being dependent on the steering influence. This multiple-copy scenario presents a new model of a one-way quantum data hiding CVQIP device. Lastly, our research showcases that when the steering influence is absent, the diagrams of the shared Gaussian states are free from sublinearity, aligning with their classical representability. Conversely, the diagrams exhibit sublinearity for non-Gaussian states sharing quantum correlations, underscoring the significance of quantum steering in remote Wigner negativity. This finding highlights the potential of quantum steering as a resource for nonclassical correlations. Moreover, the research proposes a method for directly inferring the steering influence from Alice's to Bob's systems without requiring knowledge of the shared quantum state. This influence holds key benefits for secure quantum communication and can be exploited for various applications. Ultimately, the research provides an innovative framework for understanding the connections between nonclassical correlations and their practical uses in remote Wigner negativity. Moreover, the research proposes an implementation of a quantum random number generator using a one-time pad, with Bob's measurements providing randomness that are influenced by Alice's shared quantum state. In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach called the effective vertex function, which describes the interaction between a single photon and a series of quantum systems, we can efficiently analyze multi-photon scattering problems. To verify the accuracy and practicality of our method, we apply it to two well-documented scenarios: a quantum cavity interacting with N quantum dots and a quantum cavity coupled with N quantum dot resonators via Reconfigurable Waveguide switches. Our analysis shows that this approach not only accurately determines the non-linear photon scattering problem but also identifies specific challenges associated with numerical calculations in problems involving a large number of physical systems. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of using delayed coherent quantum feedback in both schemes to enable single-photon binary gates that can circumvent these computational hurdles. Our work demonstrates that the diagrammatic method is a versatile and powerful technique for analyzing nonlinear problems in quantum systems and highlights its efficacy in designing multi-photon information processing applications. Additionally, using this approach, we derive analytical formulas for calculating the effective vertex using two different quantum feedback schemes, namely, an additional amplifier and a balanced beam splitter in a loop. Our method deviates from previous studies that used this approach in cold cavity schemes by incorporating effective vertex calculations in a warm cavity utilizing quantum feedback. Consequently, we calculate the scattering matrix for the N-phon decay process and show that it can be transformed into a linear problem when using the coherent feedback scheme with N = 100, a scenario that would otherwise require an inordinate amount of computational time without it. Our work thus broadens the scope and practicality of the diagrammatic method in a wide range of quantum system designs. Our code for this work can be found at https://github.com/Quantum-Dragon/delayed_vertex_code. Lastly, we propose an alternative scheme known as quasi-periodic phase modulation (QPM) that can provide an approximation to the scattering matrix with a substantial degree of accuracy and efficiency, thereby offering a potential coherent alternative to the balanced beam splitter in a loop (BBIS) scheme. Our analysis reveals that for N = 100, QPM allows for an accurate scattering matrix calculation with 40 years of computational time, a mere 1/100th of the time required by the BBIS scheme. Our work suggests that QPM has the potential to efficiently enhance coherent quantum feedback in quantum technologies. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero. Furthermore, it demonstrates that using Faulhaber's Formula for even Bernoulli numbers requires division by zero, which underscores the formula's validity only for odd Bernoulli numbers. As a consequence, we derive the odd Bernoulli numbers via Faulhaber's Formula. Notably, this approach avoids employing characteristic functions or other analogous concepts commonly found in characteristic-free proofs. Moreover, it is crucial to recognize that odd Bernoulli numbers cannot be calculated using the standard generating function due to the inclusion of $\frac{1}{p}$, a constant characteristic of odd Bernoulli numbers, where $p$ is a prime number. By leveraging an alternative method for calculating the Bernoulli numbers, we show that odd Bernoulli numbers can be represented as a sum of certain odd integers, thereby solving an elementary integer equation. Lastly, we utilize Faulhaber's Formula to express the odd odd Bernoulli numbers in terms of a power of two and generalize this formula for odd $A_{p-1}$ numbers, where $p$ is a prime number. By extending this formula, we can derive a power series consisting of odd terms, a concept also applicable to odd Spivek numbers. Notably, this odd Spivek power series can be utilized to identify and distinguish even Spivek numbers. Ultimately, using a characteristic-free approach, we prove that a significant generalization of the formula derived for odd Bernoulli numbers can be achieved, specifically for odd Spivek numbers with a non-zero first term. Importantly, this odd Spivek formula allows for the easy derivation of an integral representation for even Spivek numbers. As a final observation, we utilize Faulhaber's Formula to express the odd Genocchi numbers with a power of two and generalize this formula for odd $A_{p-1}$ numbers, where $p$ is a prime number. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol period of the phase reference waveform, followed by energy collection over multiple delay periods. This process effectively cancels out interference from adjacent symbols in an additive white Gaussian noise channel. Nevertheless, in scenarios where the receiver has an accurate understanding of the phase and Doppler shift, but is unaware of other parameters such as amplitude, a modified version of the conventional differential detection technique can achieve optimal performance equivalent to the original, simply by omitting the amplitude-related component from the product structure. This paper presents a direct, analytical method for finding the time-reversed version of the phase reference waveform that maintains this optimal performance. The developed analysis is complex and heavy in computational requirements, but it offers a reliable and precise method for determining optimal delay periods, which is beneficial for applications requiring short delays. The analysis is first applied in a ideal noise-free environment, then extended to consider the impact of amplitude variations. The proposed method is currently applicable to a narrow class of waveforms, such as binary offset carrier with a single amplitude value, but the techniques and tools presented can be used as a basis for extensions to more complex waveforms with multiple amplitude values. Furthermore, the analysis provides a general method for determining optimal delay periods, which can be calculated using approximate values of the interference waveform. The main body of the paper simplifies the burden of calculations, achieves a precise determination of optimal delay periods, and reduces the complexity of the analytical method. Anomaly detection without labelled data is increasingly being used to identify unusual patterns within datasets, given that manually annotating data can be impractical or costly; one such unsupervised method that has gained popularity in recent times is the Isolation Forest algorithm, which employs a random tree-based approach to compute an anomaly score through ensemble learning. However, a conventional Isolation Forest may still be optimized in terms of memory requirements, processing time, and overall performance to suit constrained systems and small-footprint AI implementations on resource-restricted microcontrollers. Additionally, anomaly detection systems typically neglect the value of user-provided feedback as a form of weak supervision in informing decision-making. To overcome these limitations and the inefficiencies in conventional Isolation Forest, we present TiWS-iForest, a method that harnesses weak supervision to simplify and enhance Isolation Forest's anomaly detection capabilities, which is then demonstrated to be effective on real-world datasets, with the accompanying code publicly available for improved replicability. Specifically, TiWS-iForest incorporates the use of user-provided feedback to streamline anomaly detection, reduces the memory and computational costs associated with Isolation Forest by at least 60%, and demonstrates improved or comparable performance on a variety of benchmark datasets when compared to a range of state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods. Finally, we present initial findings on the feasibility of adapting TiWS-iForest for real-time operation on resource-restricted microcontrollers. The results demonstrate the potential for significant reduction in the energy consumption required to support anomaly detection on microcontrollers, with the anomaly detection process itself taking no more than 45 microseconds to complete on commonly available 32-bit microcontrollers such as the STM32. The associated code for TiWS-iForest has been made publicly available on the GiT platform at the following address: https://git.io/tiwsifforest. Conversely, the code specifically tailored for microcontroller support is available on the microProcessor's GiT platform at the following address: https://git.io/tiwsifprocessor. Ultimately, the goal of TiWS-iForest is to facilitate the development of efficient anomaly detection systems that are transparent in terms of their underlying algorithms, with the results from TiWS-iForest presenting significant potential for application in a range of domains and use cases, from computer security to medical imaging and beyond. A typical approach for modelling extreme events involves considering these events as occurrences above a high threshold, often modelled using block maxima or exceedances above a constant level. This method estimates parameters based on data above a particular high threshold and treats them as constant across all thresholds, which has the advantage of simplicity but can also result in inaccurate models if the parameter changes significantly across different thresholds. To address this issue, we're proposing a solution that involves modelling the parameter as a random variable, using Bayes estimation and Monte Carlo simulations to create a pooled sample from multiple sites with shared parameters. This allows us to utilise asymptotic theory to estimate the distribution of the parameter, without being constrained by the traditional limitations of extreme value modelling. Our method has been applied to a dataset of 24 hourly excess rainfall depths recorded at 10 weather stations in Singapore, where we've considered the GEV as the candidate distribution, allowing the location parameter to vary across sites and the scale and shape parameters to be threshold-invariant. Our results indicate significant changes in the parameter values when modelling rainfall depths above certain thresholds, suggesting that the parameter does indeed remain constant above a particular high threshold, supporting our modelling approach. Our method also offers a novel application of quantitative climate mapping, where we've used Bayesian estimation to produce maps displaying the predicted distribution of parameter values across Singapore. To ensure reliable estimates, we've only included stations with a high quantity of data and large thresholds, as specified by our method. Our results include estimates of the predicted distribution of annual excess rainfall depths at specified sites and thresholds, as well as a sensitivity analysis of the influence of individual data points on the estimated parameter values. Our method demonstrates that the modelling of threshold-invariant parameters can be valuable, provided that the threshold is well-defined and supported by the data, resulting in accurate estimates and effective modelling. To take advantage of the availability of a large quantity of data and the sharing of common parameters, our method offers significant benefits when modelling extreme events. Our method has broad applications, as the modelling framework can be easily extended to accommodate other parameterisation scenarios and the method can also be adapted for use with other parametric families of distributions. Our code is available online for reference. Our results also highlight some issues with modelling and offer some insights into the frequency of extreme rainfall events in Singapore. Our method has significant implications for water management practices, as the estimated parameters can be used to inform design decisions and support operational activities such as reservoir releases, as well as provide a framework for assessing the risk of extreme water shortages. Moreover, the cluster's first population stars displayed lower iron content and shorter aluminosity measurements compared to those with higher iron content. Notably, the variation in iron content within the rich globular cluster Omega Centauri follows an intricate pattern, with different iron levels correlated with varying aluminosity measurements across its subpopulations. These correlations suggest that internal dynamics likely contributed to the formation of the cluster's second population stars, particularly those with varying metallicity, despite initial attempts to uniformize their composition. Our research produces calculations for the pressure, trace of the energy-momentum tensor, speed of sound and lattice character at the physical point. We also examine and compare various methods for estimating the finite volume correction to the speed of sound. Furthermore, using the fact that the trace of the energy-momentum tensor is finite in QCD, we identify a source of inaccuracy in the steepest descent method that results in a small artificial change in the speed of sound equation of state between successive volumes. We explore the grounds for removing finite volume corrections to the speed of sound, as has been done in nearly all QCD simulations at a given volume. We also write down formulas for calculating renormalization group invariants from the time-like correlator's asymptotic properties, and demonstrate how this can lead to additional insights into corrections to the speed of sound, particularly when the lattice constant becomes increasingly small. Our research produces high-precision calculations at the physical point, but we focus our comparisons with experimental results to a range of pion masses between 310 to 450 MeV. We include various appendices with additional details on topics, including calculations, implementation details and broader context. Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Rocket Group are developing an innovation that can filter out this unwanted radiation, enabling high-precision observations in space. The new technology, originally used on planetary missions, can now be incorporated into near-Earth orbiting satellites, and our team is refining this cell for application in various UVS spacecraft, including the Voyager missions. The absorption cells containing molecular species like ozone and water can eliminate over 90% of radiation in specific frequencies. To achieve this, we are fine-tuning bandwidths to target particular frequencies while maintaining the cells' original structure. The updated technology will significantly benefit accurate far ultraviolet space-based observations. Moreover, we are exploring a novel approach, known as photochemical control, that uses light to trigger chemical reactions within the cell and enhance absorption rates. This technique could further improve signal suppression by up to 10% in certain cases. The concept of photochemical control may also lead to new research opportunities in basic science applications. Our research is currently focusing on implementing photochemical control in various cell designs, and preliminary results indicate its potential as a versatile tool for space-based observation in the far ultraviolet range. By manipulating the cells' absorption properties, we can achieve accurate readings of celestial objects, and our research could contribute to upcoming UVS spacecraft, including the JAXA Life, the NASA PACE, and the ESA-ADT missions. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a brief code, and a tree-like data structure that stores code variations, along with their original image file locations. Prior image detection and retrieval methods have been restricted to pairwise comparisons, with each code being linked to a single image. We have developed a novel technique, referred to as NIFTRE, that allows multi-pathage connections between the code and tree structure, thereby enhancing retrieval and detection performance. To achieve this, NIFTRE leverages a data structure that allows for the identification of most similar codes, including those obtained from new, composite images. Comprehensive testing on popular image databases such as CubicWeb, OxfordII, and MS-Coco, among others, demonstrates significant performance improvements for NIFTRE compared to state-of-the-art image detection and retrieval methods. For certain image datasets, for instance, NIFTRE exhibits a significant 52% improvement in average recall rate at given false positive rates, or a 53% improvement in precision at given recall rates. Further details on NIFTRE, including its code and pre-trained models, can be found online. Images provided by Eric Talton were used for testing and evaluation purposes. This study confirms that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in
Gaussian noise environments, with the caveat that an all-knowing adversary cannot be
beated. An examination of a model comprising encoder, decoder, and adversary was
carried out, with the latter possessing unlimited transmission capabilities and
unlimited access to the transmitted message. It was demonstrated that modifying an
existing communication protocol can enable secure transmission with negligible
efficiency loss, providing an attacker with negligible benefits. A measurement
metric quantifying the adversary's advantage was defined, and the bounds on this
metric were defined in terms of the degree to which the transmitter and receiver
are connected. An examination of this metric revealed a trade-off between the level
of authentication and the reliability of the transmission. Authentication was found
to be feasible with an adversary's gain limited to 1.03, but this number can rise
in scenarios with reduced degrees of freedom between the transmitter and receiver.
An alternative method of authentication, involving a trusted third party, was also
investigated in order to demonstrate that this method does not contradict the
results obtained for the single-entity model. Moreover, physical layer-based
authentication via a physical channel was found to be impossible regardless of the
type of communication (discrete or continuous) because an attacker can mimic
transmissions with acceptable fidelity by recording and replaying a portion of
the transmission, even though the authenticated model's metrics do not quantify the
adversary's ability to create high-fidelity replicas. Consequently, methods of
authentication based solely on physical layer mechanisms are inadequate and should
be considered imperfect.
