Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most CT systems use polychromatic X-ray sources rather than monochromatic ones, integrating fan-beam CT with a multi-spectral analysis based on different energy levels poses considerable challenges. This is because the standard equations used in fan-beam CT do not directly apply to energy-specific datasets. In our previous research, we developed a raw CT data model that separates attenuation and attenuation-related variations from actual material densities. We subsequently extended this model to accommodate various X-ray energy levels and, specifically, the fan-beam CT mode. This led to a new CT reconstruction equation that we will discuss in detail. In our analysis, we will consider how using various energy levels affects CT and introduce two new types of image distortion: attenuation-related variations crossing with direction of X-ray beam and linking variations. We will provide numerical examples demonstrating that, under certain conditions, these distortions may cause streaking artifacts. To mitigate these distortifications, we developed an attenuation-related variations correction method. In our numerical examples, we demonstrated that, in both air-tight and water-filled cylinders scanned using different energy levels, our new method successfully minimizes crossing distortions and links distortions, demonstrating accuracy on par with conventional CT reconstruction. Our findings show that utilizing multi-spectral analyses based on different energy levels in fan-beam CT requires modification to standard equations used in conventional CT reconstruction. This leads to the introduction of new distortion types and design requirements for separating various attenuation-related variations. Moreover, cross-linking distortions in fan-beam CT are significantly more pronounced than corresponding linking distortions in parallel beam CT. Our research provides the first theoretical model partitioning various attenuation-related variations across different energy levels in fan-beam CT. Our findings may pave the way for an automatic separation of actual material densities from raw CT data and compensate for crossing distortions, thereby enhancing raw data-based CT reconstruction. In addition, our new CT reconstruction equation serves as a solid foundation for designing raw CT reconstruction systems. Our research contributes significantly to both theoretical and practical aspects of multi-spectral analysis-based CT reconstruction. Our numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of our new method for compensating distortion and reducing residual noise. When dealing with multi-variable data that follows this framework, we anticipate observing intricate connections and correlations between different components over time. Our approach to understanding and analyzing these complex interdependencies involves creating predictive models that generate future expectations, incorporating time-related factors into a framework for describing probability distributions. With an emphasis on linear assumptions, traditional multivariate analysis techniques are well-suited for handling time series data in contexts where relationships between variables remain relatively stable over time. Conversely, representations based solely on variable relationships without regard to time do not offer a complete understanding and can be inadequate, as observed in our example involving daily Amazon stock prices. Our proposed methodology focuses on distinguishing between meaningful and insignificant correlations in time series data, utilizing a two-stage process that first generates predictions through a linear model and then employs a correction mechanism to capture correlations that arise in context. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as analyzing these records can enhance healthcare quality and efficiency. To measure the effectiveness of EHR analysis, a relevant evaluation benchmark is necessary. In response, Clinical Question Answering (CQA) has been developed as a performance indicator, focusing on assessing completed clinical questions using regularized superposition of m-values. However, CQA requires significant computational resources, particularly to process a single question. To overcome this challenge, a scalable method for approximating CQA of regular clinical questions in large datasets has been proposed. This approach involves dividing the question into simpler sub-questions and using existing models to estimate the results, by representing each question as a mixture of these sub-questions. This technique has been evaluated on two public datasets, CQA and MIMIC-III, and has shown a high degree of accuracy in processing large datasets, successfully reducing computational time. By achieving a 10-fold decrease in processing time without compromising accuracy, this method demonstrates its ability to scale for large datasets. Additionally, code for this method can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/mixedmarriage/CQA_approx. We believe that this technique has the potential to further accelerate improvements in medical research. As the volume and complexity of data continue to grow, the need for effective and scalable methods to analyze these records will become increasingly crucial. In the future, this method could be expanded to include more advanced language capabilities, such as natural language processing, and integration with decision-making systems to enhance its effectiveness. Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electrostatic potential in a binary electrolyte solution in close proximity to a charged surface. By applying a method similar to that of Stillinger, we calculate the density of ions near the surface, then use these results to determine the non-linear influence of solvent effects on the electrostatic potential. From this approach, we find that at close range to a charged surface, solvent effects significantly contribute to the overall electric potential, resulting in substantially reduced electric fields compared to the predictions made by the Poisson-Boltzmann model. Furthermore, we discover that the combination of using the Michaelie level of density functional theory to model non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects leads to a more accurate match with existing laboratory data, ultimately providing a more detailed understanding of electrostatic phenomena in particular contexts, such as near mesoporous materials or in organic solvents. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and their interconnections via orbital degeneracy on the Fermi surface. By employing density functional theory to calculate the underlying band structures and integrating this analysis with the numerical results of the (Gauge-invariant) Friedel oscillations, we have thoroughly examined the properties of various magnetic atoms on Al(111) surfaces. Our predicted orbital-dependent YSR spectra exhibit exceptional agreement with experimental observations. This newly designed theoretical approach not only enhances our understanding of unconventional superconductor--impurity interactions, but it also enables the precise identification of magnetic impurity orbitals on a wide variety of superconducting surfaces. Furthermore, these findings provide valuable insights for the development of (quantum dot-based) quantum processors, which rely on the unique interactions between magnetic impurities and superconducting materials. Ultimately, these findings hold potential for the design of efficient qubit systems in which orbital degeneracy plays a pivotal role. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects. However, techniques like NDT struggle in scenes where there are changes in view. To tackle this, deep learning-based approaches have been developed to register point clouds from different views. While some of these methods capitalize on existing point cloud filters to register dynamic scenes, they rely on external features not inherent to the point cloud itself. Other methods use a coarse-to-fine approach to estimate distributions or maps from point clouds, but this requires many training examples. To overcome these limitations, a new method called PCD2 is proposed, which relies on a novel neural transformation to register dynamic scenes. PCD2 uses a novel neural transformation to map open3d point cloud vectors to corresponding vector normals, and then uses a depth estimate correlation loss to estimate depth in addition to existing losses. Experiments show that PCD2 surpasses competing distribution-to-distribution point cloud registration techniques with and without deep learning components. Furthermore, PCD2 remains resilient to missing data, a problem many distribution-to-distribution point cloud registration methods struggle with. PCD2 remains efficient through the use of a point cloud vector and normal vector transformation that relies on the properties of a 3 by 3 kernel used to estimate correspondence. Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, these methods excel when evaluating internal 
performance but struggle when assessing external validity, including generalizing 
to unrelated datasets and evaluating model reliability after deployment. This 
paper addresses these challenges by integrating statistical metrics into common 
deep learning architectures to enhance validation of satellite image models. 
To test our proposed method, we utilized high-level semantic segmentation of 
ribs in bovine carcasses from aerial images, applying our new method to assess 
the performance of deep learning models after deployment. Evaluation results 
reveal a significant enhancement in model reliability assessments, up to 240%, 
and highlight the importance of statistical metrics for evaluating real-world 
application datasets. Moreover, the paper contributes to the fields of 
satellite image and computational livestock sensing by achieving state-of-the-
art performance in n=5 predictions and achieving a high $F_1$ score of 0.9163. 
Codes are publicly available at https://github.com/marcosgorce/rib_corr.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics close to the Fermi level.

To develop an enhanced understanding of electronic dynamics under high-fluence conditions, researchers have created a simplified theoretical model, based on recognized physical principles, to elucidate how electronic processes progress. The model examines distinct physical phenomena such as resonance absorption, non-resonance absorption, electron scattering, thermalization of valence bands, and stimulated emission. The model demonstrates a straightforward approach to elucidating how each of these processes affects changes observed in XANES measurements.

When the density of states is not taken into consideration, the model correlates well with experimental findings for metallic nickel, showing good consistency over a vast fluence range exceeding three orders of magnitude. The findings suggest that at high fluences, electron scattering dominates, whereas at lower fluences, stimulated emission, resonance absorption, and electron interactions contribute significantly. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it's exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We examine the potential of 
continual learning in making the MSL segmentation process more automatic and
efficient. We also examine the impact of different continual learning methods 
on the model's performance compared to traditional training methods in relation
to lesion segmentation accuracy, using eight different hospital datasets. 
Utilizing an HCPC dataset initially, we train models using various strategies
such as curriculum learning, progressive learning, finite-domain learning and
 gradient based learning. The results show that continual learning leads to a 
significantly lower decline in segmentation performance compared to traditional
methods when using datasets from different hospitals, resulting in more accurate 
lesion segmentation. Notably, the models trained using curriculum learning and 
gradient based learning perform better on average compared to the control group 
in terms of accurate lesion segmentation. Importantly, the models trained using
continual learning methods display similar performance to models trained on a
single dataset from a specific hospital in terms of accurate lesion segmentation,
without needing extensive training on that particular dataset. This suggests that
continual learning in the context of MSL segmentation for different hospitals can
be just as effective as traditional methods of having access to a large dataset 
from a single hospital. The research supports the use of continual learning as a
potential solution for making the MSL segmentation process more automatic and
efficient. Alongside this, the research proposes developing more advanced
continual learning methods for the purpose of future applications. 
Continual learning may have important implications for future applications as
well, especially when dealing with data from diverse hospital networks in the
future.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are notably more massive, exceeding their starless counterparts by nearly an order of magnitude, a phenomenon not readily explained by the core mass function.  Further examination of core mass distributions across different regions of the Dragon cloud further complicates the association between core mass and stellar mass.  It appears that outflow emitting cores are more widely dispersed throughout the cloud in contrast to the centrally concentrated distribution of these outflow emitting regions.  Therefore, rather than a gradual development of stars within the cloud, our data suggests the existence of distinct protostellar population born from more massive cores within specific sub-regions of the cloud.  Consequently, a straightforward model of core mass evolution from starless to protostellar is challenged.  Moreover, the mass difference between protostellar starless cores within the cloud implies diversity in the initiation of stellar formation.  Finally, the analysis highlights the limitations of statistical inferences regarding the formation of stars due to the complicated nature of the spatial distribution of the considered sample.  It is hoped that future studies of similar statistical inferences, inevitably present in future data, are not taken for granted. The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for the destruction of black holes during a star's evolution. Our results show a significant decrease in the predicted number of PBH-related microlensing events when a star's mass exceeds 9 times the mass of our sun. This threshold serves as a boundary, revealing that up to 40% of our galaxy's stellar mass can be attributed to primordial black holes without affecting the predicted microlensing frequency. However, the remaining 60% of our galaxy's stellar mass still allows for a detectable number of PBH-related microlensing events. Additionally, we found that observing the variation in the PBH microlensing frequency as it relates to galactic specific stellar masses could help us determine the relevance of primordial black holes as a possible form of dark matter. Our study also enables the prediction of the theoretical minimum and maximum values of PBH-related microlensing frequency for galaxies with masses within particular ranges. These findings are accessible through an online public database. Our analysis of the theoretical estimates of the gravitational lensing activity displayed by 1346 galaxies from the SDSS database reveals no notable difference between the observed and predicted PBH-related microlensing frequencies. This discrepancy may suggest that either primordial black holes cannot constitute a significant form of dark matter or they must have formed from normal stellar bodies through a process of black hole formation. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with
improved performance and a significant reduction in parameters at a mere 0.09% of fine-tuning cost. 
The code for PASTA is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/alexmenotti/parameter-efficient-tuning-in-bert. 
Our experiments cover a broad spectrum of NLU tasks and utilize various popular pre-trained models, including BERT, BART, and RoBERTa. 
A thorough comparison on XNLI, CoLA, SST-2, TACRED, and NER tasks shows PASTA outperforms existing techniques, like BERT-LF, EFFNET, and SHUFFLE, by an average of 1.24 points in XNLI accuracy metric. Moreover, PASTA's performance surpasses recent state-of-the-art methods EFFNET and MPT in a multi-task evaluation, considering a weighted average of task-specific performances on TACRED and SST-2.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, distinguishing them involves how they combine added components with the core collection. By conducting experiments on real-world datasets, we adapt various retrieval approaches to transform the problem into a contrastive learning task, utilizing a similarity measure to compare initial and enlarged collections. Our analysis of the results suggests that incorporating added items in a sequential manner yields better performance compared to concurrent addition. Furthermore, we offer theoretical justification for why contrastive learning is effective in this context, based on how added items influence the similarity score, which serves as a key metric in preference modeling. The proposed approach demonstrates superiority to existing methods, according to our experiments. Moreover, when the problem is reformulated as a contrastive learning task, it becomes possible to utilize an efficient and unbiased estimator for measuring the impact of added items. To the best of our knowledge, this paper encompasses the most comprehensive exploration of context-dependent preference modeling, encompassing comprehensive treatments of preference handling, suitable function types, and added item integration. Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this from two angles: by assessing a model's ability to identify a sentence as negative, and by evaluating its understanding of negated sentence meanings. Our analysis indicates that models fall short in both areas. A notable finding reveals that models are better at recognizing individual words with negative meanings than Negated Word Sense Evaluation counterparts. Our explanation for these results is that language models learn to process complex meanings from co-occurrences, which can lead to errors when it comes to negated meanings. We conclude that contemporary natural language processing models remain unsuitable for complex human reasoning tasks, especially those that involve negation. Further work should focus on creating more precise measures of language comprehension and developing more sophisticated models that can grasp nuanced meanings. We hope that our research lays the groundwork for an understanding of the language models' shortcomings and informs the design of more human-like language processing systems. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by designing a novel, bidirectional attention model capable of simultaneous analysis of source and previous target sequences. This model can be efficiently implemented by combining source and previous target sequence embeddings into the traditional neural machine translation framework, thus making source and previous target sequence information accessible to the attention model equally. Experimental results show that by incorporating the proposed bidirectional attention model, significant performance improvements can be achieved, ranging from 1 to 4.5 relative points, on three different language pairs. Additionally, the model's benefits are highlighted through detailed analysis of source and previous target sequence attention maps. Furthermore, it is suggested that the bidirectional attention model can serve as a foundation for exploring further insights related to target word generation. Moreover, the proposed model resolves the limitations of existing research in this area, underpinned by theoretical frameworks in both statistical machine translation and deep learning domains. Detailed explanations and underlying assumptions are presented in the paper. To facilitate future research, the complete source code and the experimental data have been made publicly available. We hope that the proposed model can contribute to advancements in both traditional and deep neural machine translation areas. Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies. For instance, our formula reduces the required grid size by half compared to the original theorem when applied to the lognormal model. Through a straightforward modification, we extend this theory to suit options involving multiple assets, detailing specific examples for power options, average options with barriers, and deterministic interest rates. Furthermore, we present a universal penalized explicit Laplace transform for power options, serving as a foundation for pricing time-delayed options. Closely related to the classical power series expansion, this penalization represents an innovative aspect of the presented theory and could be valuable for options lacking closed-form solutions. High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored from both a
theoretical and computational perspective. These models play a vital role in
understanding complex macroeconomic and financial systems by identifying key
common factors that influence numerous observed time series. Focusing on large
datasets, our analysis covers the estimation, evaluation, and optimization of
these models, highlighting notable recent advancements. Moreover, our study
emphasizes the practical implementation of these models using relevant R packages.
This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of theoretical concepts and
associated computational methods, as well as considering challenging research
questions and relevant reasons for exploring these models. In particular, we
examine the constraints of these models and propose possible solutions, all
while acknowledging intriguing open questions in this field. Lastly, we
consider potential avenues for future exploration in High-Dimensional Dynamic
Factor Models. By offering an in-depth analysis of these models, our study
aspires to make cutting-edge computational methods more accessible to a broader
audience. Moreover, our analysis seeks to highlight the advantages of using
computational tools to support theoretical advancements in this field. In total,
twenty-one papers published between 2007 and 2020 are reviewed and assessed. 
Ultimately, our review seeks to provide a detailed understanding of the
complexity of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models and to highlight active
research areas and potential developments in this field. 
To read more about the computational aspects of these models, please refer to 
the contributed paper titled "Inference and Simulation for High-Dimensional Dynamic
Factor Models: An Overview of Recent Developments and Future Challenges". 
That paper can be found along with this review on an online platform.

The evidence presented demonstrates that key properties of the classical Thompson groups are preserved, albeit in a revised form, among their braided counterparts. The underlying reasoning relies on an examination of quasistability in their associated $S$-sets. This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been made publicly available on the HuggingFace Transformers library. A notable achievement is the development of a faster and more robust retrieval method, which outperforms existing solutions. The specific RAG architecture used in our experiments comprises a dense retrieval cross-attention layer and a generator language model. Our results show that pre-training the retrieval and fine-tuning the entire RAG model yields significant enhancements in the context of question answering. The end-to-end RAG architecture and associated code have been designed to facilitate easy replication and experimentation. A public dataset has been used for training and testing, namely the SQuAD 1.1 dataset. However, the RAG architecture has the potential to be applied in various other NLP tasks beyond question answering. A notable limitation of our architecture is the potential for memory constraints on cloud-based platforms, which may give rise to inaccurate readings on the performance. Moreover, a higher computational cost is required to achieve the end-to-end RAG architecture, which one-sided affects downstream performance. The potential exists for further improvements to be made in the end-to-end RAG architecture. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantNow/End-to-End-RAG. This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of a recently developed asymptotic tractability of trigonometric moment problems when $k$ is large. This similar approach also works for the Chebyshev weight $-\frac{2}{2-x}$, albeit under slightly modified circumstances. As an extension, we investigate certain properties of the associated Fermon-James polynomials, cosmological polynomials, and we find new ways to approximate certain complex integrals by polynomial truncations. These trigonometric moment problems, which are known to be equivalently formulated as Grassmannian recursion problems, are now shown to be solvable only when the internal parameters $k$ and $\nu$ are both sufficiently large. Moreover, this investigation reveals a previously unknown connection between the generated logarithmic orthogonal polynomials, cosmological polynomials, and their relation to the Tchebychev polynomials, achieved through the implementation of a shift operation. This relation is so contrived that for large values of $k$, both the logarithmic orthogonal polynomials and the Tchebychev polynomials exhibit identical behavior, though this comes at the expense of lesser closeness for intermediate values of $k$ in relation to $k\rightarrow\infty$. As a consequence of the obtained asymptotic formulas, these logarithmic orthogonal polynomials can effectively be approximated by polynomial truncations of Tchebychev polynomials, with known accuracy, and we propose a new criterion for determining when a trigonometric weight is suitable for constructing such a sequence of approximations, as an extension to a similar inquiry previously posed by A. Magnus. As an additional discovery, we find that cosmological polynomials enjoy certain properties of symmetry, as well as their relation to the exclusion principle, when defined over the interval $(-1,1)$. Moreover, we express the cosine-cosine P\'olya-Ferguson-Fermat polynomials in relation to the logarithmic orthogonal polynomials and we verify certain equivalences in their generated recurrence relations. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval primarily utilize pre-trained vision backbones with rigid network architectures, thereby hindering the ability to further refine the video representation and yielding suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we present TS2-Net, a groundbreaking transformer architecture incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, which effectively tailors token sequences to capture the intricate movements in videos and pinpoint critical spatial and temporal details. The TS2-Net's adaptability in shifting token features across frames preserves comprehensive token information, and its token selection mechanism efficiently isolates semantically vital tokens from input videos. Thoroughly evaluating TS2-Net on major text-video retrieval benchmarks has led to exceptional performance, setting new records on MSRVTT, VATEX, LSMDC, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo. For instance, it surpasses the previous best MSRVTT results by 7.8% (R@1) under a family setting. We showcase the efficacy of TS2-Net's token selection in comprehensive visualization experiments. In our proposed network science research, a new type of network is suggested which blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment. This involves each newly joining nodes selecting, with given probabilities, either the preferential attachment rule or the uniform attachment rule, to add edges to existing nodes. The resulting network exhibits a mix of the characteristics seen in networks formed entirely by preferential attachment and those formed entirely by uniform attachment. Specifically, it shows a switch between exponential and 1/f behavior in the distribution of node degrees and demonstrates a transition from temporal to asymptotic dependence in the distribution of largest components, despite following a universal pattern for all time. Moreover, underlying this behavior is a fundamental balance between two opposing forces: on one hand the tendency for hubs to attract and retain edges and, on the other hand, the tendency for hubs to lose edges. Using a branching and linking framework we develop a rigorous mathematical analysis which reveals a wide range of fundamental properties of this type of network, including the exponential distribution of largest components, the asymptotic dependence of the largest component and the degree distribution near the transition point and detailed estimates for all time. Furthermore, we develop a simple and universal method to compute the asymptotics and further research is needed to explore applications, extensions and related questions. This branch-and-link approach may also be useful in analyzing other network creation processes. For instance, networks formed by a mixture of preferential attachment and preferential attachment with degree exponent, could be a special case in our theorem, when one of the exponents is 2. Such a problem will be explored in separate research, including simulations to capture the transition from temporal to asymptotic dependence. The simulations will reveal additional information before proving them. Moreover, an additional simulation will explore the impact of varying the parameters of the uniform attachment rule, specifically when nodes attach with degree k to existing nodes, where k varies. The resulting networks will exhibit a pattern of nodes grouped in clusters based on their degree and each person's movement will be characterised by a random walk. This random walk will be analysed in terms of the time it takes for a new node to reach a high degree node and the efficiency of this process will be evaluated based on these time measurements. Simulations will also reveal patterns in the layering of this type of network and these patterns will be compared with other well-known models. The framework's performance under various scavenging techniques is compared, revealing its ability to achieve accurate detection with minimal data loss. All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at boosting the accuracy of AI systems by enhancing their detection and correction of error-producing patterns. Specifically, this approach focuses on bolstering pattern recognition and processing techniques to effectively identify and rectify patterns that contain critical inconsistencies or inconsistencies significant to the task, based on the analysis of human error patterns for tasks such as image segmentation in medical imaging. Building on human expertise for correcting AI errors facilitates aligned AI-learning processes, thereby demonstrating the potential for sustainable, self-regulating AI performance improvement. This report shares findings on evaluating this approach, demonstrating comparable human error rates to state-of-the-art medical imaging models and highlighting that both AI and human errors frequently involve similar task-related flaws. Ultimately, this research provides evidence for an efficient, AI-driven mechanism to prevent and rectify errors. Moreover, it suggests that future AI systems can effectively manage and respond to their own errors using their own capabilities and capabilities modeled after human processes. This report proposes a general framework for preserving and enhancing AI quality over long periods. Moreover, it facilitates responsible AI development, including transparent algorithms that inform operators about their limitations and contribute to public awareness. Finally, this research lays the foundational knowledge to investigate the ethical implications of AI errors and how to mitigate them. By introducing a spin-orbit coupling factor γ, we observe the emergence of finite-phased states as γ increases. Through numerical simulations of the associated Lagrangian, we identify key phase transition thresholds at low temperatures. Notably, our findings indicate that the required interaction intensity to transition from superfluid to Mott insulator decreases with greater γ, while the condensate fraction exhibits an inverse relationship with Rashba coupling under these conditions. Furthermore, we discover a new phase characterized by finite momentum condensation, forming when γ falls within a specific range. To better understand this phenomenon, we carry out a mean-field analysis to determine phase diagrams at zero temperature. Our results show that the phase with finite momentum condensation is favorably positioned at γ values between 0.5 and 1.0. Additionally, we have developed a simplified model to describe the phase transition involving the formation of chiral vortices, which occurs at high Rashba coupling levels and competes with the phase transition involving the formation of chiral vortices. If you're interested in a more in-depth understanding, please refer to the associated paper, "Phases of a Bose-Hubbard gas with spin-orbit coupling," which is now available online. 

To confirm our predictions, we suggest conducting an experiment where you create a ring of Rb atoms using a Rydberg pump and then apply a specific laser pulse to trigger the phase transition and observe the resulting behavior. You can use spatial resolution to distinguish between different phases, while rotating an applied magnetic field will allow you to detect the formation of chiral vortices. Using a technique called edge singularities to analyze the boundary of the images will enable you to quantify the angular momentum of the condensate, thereby quantifying the orbital occupation of the phase. Our proposed research design is generally applicable to other cold quantum gases featuring spin-orbit coupling, such as those derived from fermions, and may result in new methods for creating and manipulating topological phases at zero temperature. 

In the field of quantum information processing, topological phases at zero temperature are generally realizable and can be destroyed by applying either heat or particle decay. Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of a group G_1 degrading to group G_2, which is investigated within this research. Graph degeneration is found to encompass a particular instance of this group relationship. The paper examines unique properties arising from graph degeneration. To visualize this, it employs a diagrammatic approach representing graphs realized by finite abelian groups. Order relationships within a set of all such graphs realized by finite abelian groups, based on different prime numbers, are also studied. Moreover, it is demonstrated that each finite abelian group of a particular rank corresponds to chains within a poset structure. Finally, a mathematical expression is developed representing the degree of a projective representation of a symmetric group, and this formula determines the number of distinct saturated chains within this poset structure and the diversity of finite abelian groups by their order values. Lastly, it is demonstrated that each finite abelian group of a particular rank possesses a significant number of distinct saturated chains. To further validate the feasibility of this problem, an algorithm is designed to identify pairs of finite abelian groups that exhibit a particular order relationship. Furthermore, the distribution and proportionality of such pairs are analyzed using methods from number theory. Specifically, the research explores their distribution along the prime number spectrum and establishes a particular order relationship within a set of pairs, based on their corresponding group orders. It is discovered that, for n > 2, the proportion of finite abelian groups by their order, based on a set of prime numbers, exhibits a consistent and uniform pattern. Lastly, statistical insights into the diversity of projective representation structures of large symmetric groups are investigated, revealing consistent and uniform proportionality, based on a set of distinct group orders. To further validate these findings, an algorithm was designed to identify and collect a representative sample of finite abelian groups by their order. This research provides a diagrammatic representation of graphs realized by their order. Specifically, the number of such graphs, based on their order, is calculated and found to adhere to a consistent and uniform pattern. It is demonstrated that similar consistency exists within a set of pairs, based on their order, for a particular mathematical expression associated with symmetric groups. Consequently, the research provides a significant number of distinct saturated chains for a particular poset structure and the number of distinct projective representation structures of a large symmetric group.

background interference will hinder accurate data analysis and detector
operation unless mitigated. Research focuses on reducing BIB in detector design,
including triggering, data processing, and analysis stages. Studies were carried
out on a detector utilizing a tungsten nose-cone to filter BIB for a 1.5 TeV
energy threshold. In-depth analysis targeted the innermost detector sections with

tracker segments, and implementing thin-pigged scintillator inserts. Each concept
demonstrated substantial BIB reduction capabilities, particularly effective in
poly-crystalline Cesium Iodide sensors offering a 2D direction indication and
significant 80% reduction in BIB. Such designs not only streamline design
processes but also provide a reduced detector thickness with maintained
performance, thereby contributing to the development of efficient muon colliders.

This dynamic balance enables initial exploration of various sparsity patterns and gradually shifts towards optimizing parameters with respect to a predetermined sparsity pattern. To achieve this goal, test code must be designed with high quality standards similar to the original code. Test smells present an obstacle to this objective, compromising the quality of test code. A test smell is an indicator that a specific part of a test needs adjustment. To address this issue, researchers developed TSEasts, a metric that quantifies how prone a test is to various test smells by analyzing its structure and the elements present in the test code. To demonstrate its usefulness, the framework was applied to two open-source projects. The results suggest that projects with higher TSEasts scores are more susceptible to test smells. We introduce the updated version of the {\tt KKMCee} event generator, version 5.00.2, designed for simulating lepton-lepton, W and Z boson production via high-energy electron-positron annihilation, and their subsequent decays, at the energy range spanning from 0 to 1050 GeV. Built upon the {\tt PGS} parton shower algorithm, the event generator incorporates state-of-the-art Feynman graph evaluations via the {\tt FORM} computational algebra system, augmented with self-interacting W and Z boson width calculations, accounted for by a specialized routine. As an advanced kinematic generator, it accounts for lepton mass effects, aligns with modern particle data book values, and offers polarized anihilation options, vector-boson polarization simulation, and comprehensive decay processes for final-state leptons, lepton-neutron, lepton-waiton, and lepton decays. Notably, its core code has been restructured to conform to the {\tt GENEVA} framework, enabling seamless integration with popular next-generation fast detectors, such as the future FCC-ee experiment. Our research demonstrates the generator's capabilities by evaluating its predictions against recent precision measurements of the Z boson lineshape and the differential distributions of the luminosity-measurening ALEPH process. The generator is now publicly accessible via the CERN CERLWEB repository (webhep.hep.ui). \\

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion artifact and make ECG signals more interpretable even during high-impact motion. By achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation, this approach accelerates diagnostic processes and achieves better results. Notably, our technique has successfully estimated IBIs from ECG signals with signal-to-noise ratios of up to -30 decibels and achieved average root mean square error of 13 milliseconds. Moreover, the percentage error of IBI estimates remains under 8%, surpassing existing benchmarks. A live comparison of this approach against current state-of-the-art techniques using deep learning for IBI estimation and ECG signal denoising shows our technique achieves significant improvements in the form of lower RMSE and percentage error while being much faster. The source code for our solution is available at https://github.com/berkeley-yes/MotionArtifactRemovalECG, where further advancements and refinements to our technique are anticipated. The proposed method represents a significant advancement in achieving accurate denoising and IBI estimation and has the potential to be applied in wearable devices and remote health monitoring systems to facilitate early detection of cardiovascular diseases. The study's findings highlight the effectiveness of our solution, achieving average IBI estimates within 13 milliseconds and percentage error below 8%, which is far superior to existing approaches. Network analytics extensively employs dynamic graph embedding, which enables the conversion of complex dynamic graphs into simplified representations suitable for analysis and prediction. This process has widespread applications in, among others, link prediction and identity recovery. The field of dynamic graph embedding is diverse, encompassing methods that employ node features, such as temporal sequences, to create embedded node representations. In contrast, other existing methods only account for the topological structure of dynamic graphs. Despite the significant impact of time-varying network topology on embedded node representations, few methods consider this factor. This paper develops a novel approach, Temporal Topological Embedding (T2-Graph), to capture both the temporal features and the evolving network connections. T2-Graph uses a dual pathway to adjust the embedded node representations in accordance with the temporal features and the topology of the network. This approach's efficacy is demonstrated through its application on three real-world datasets, including the prediction of node-identity, link-prediction, and the identification of a knowledge-graph entity, yielding results that outperform competing methods. The source-code for T2-Graph is available at https://github.com/ranveeragrawal82/T2-Graph. This approach has been successfully implemented and tested. Initially, we employed the paradigm of a pay-per-click system to optimize T2-Graph's hyper-parameters, achieving a significant reduction in hyper-parameter tuning time. Specifically, we successfully extracted 50-dimensional embeddings for the Stanford Social Network (SSN) in 0.052 seconds, reduced this to 0.024 seconds for the 128-dimensional LinkedIn dataset, and 0.036 seconds for the 128-dimensional YouTube dataset. In addition to these applications, we also conducted a thorough investigation of various embedding methods for dynamic graphs, thereby contributing to the advancement of this field. In our experiments, we observed that different embedding methods exhibit distinct performance characteristics while also influencing the overall prediction accuracy, underscoring the need for careful method and hyper-parameter selection when designing dynamic graph applications. To facilitate future research, we have made available our approach and implementation under an open-source project on GitHub, specifically at https://github.com/ranveeragrawal82/T2-Graph. In addition, we have published our results online for reproducibility, at https://ranveeragrawal82.github.io/T2-Graph/, thereby making freely accessible embedded node representations for various datasets. In various fields of scientific inquiry, a common challenge exists in assessing the effects of interventions on multiple units and outcomes of different scales, such as binary, count, and continuous values. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that combines multiple univariate time series models with a multivariate framework. This approach accounts for inter-temporal and cross-sectional relationships among outcomes, as well as differential effects of interventions across units. To enable efficient computation, we employ a variational approximation technique. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to three real-world datasets. Notably, we utilize it to re-examine the effects of remote learning on student outcomes in a large-scale trial setting, and investigate the differences in outcomes based on various demographic factors. Furthermore, we examine the effects of targeted interventions aimed at specific units, and explore the effects of remote learning on various outcomes, including academic performance and mental health. The code and pre-specified analysis procedures are made publicly available to facilitate future research. Our results suggest that remote learning has a substantial, albeit uneven, impact across different outcomes and demographic groups, highlighting the importance of considering multiple outcomes when evaluating the effects of interventions. To streamline the process, we provide step-by-step instructions and code snippets detailing how to leverage established time series methods for estimating intervention effects across multiple outcomes. By addressing these challenges, our method opens up new avenues for the comprehensive evaluation of interventions using time series data. These developments have significant implications for future research designs, specifically in how to enhance the sensitivity of outcomes based on a priori specified outcome hierarchies. Ultimately, our method holds promise for the effective use of time series methods in causal inference and informs researchers on strategies for strategically selecting outcomes for future research studies. To illustrate this, we calculate the sample size requirements for a hypothetical pre-experimental study and show how incorporating multivariate outcomes could yield up to a 20-fold increase in the required sample size compared to a univariate framework, depending on the specified number of outcomes. Notably, our method also allows researchers to leverage multivariate methods to devise targeted interventions tailored to specific units, as exemplified by our findings regarding individualized face-to-face versus remote learning interventions. Given its extensibility to numerous time series methods, our novel approach provides a versatile platform for handling a diverse range of outcomes and unit-level effects, as well as varying contextual factors. Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of star positions, parallax, and motion based on uniform photometric data, thus enabling the determination of accurate cluster membership probabilities. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, located 2345+/-108 parsecs away and 899.5+/-0.5 deg in sky position, our research leverages Gaia DR2 to derive valuable cluster metrics such as radial profile, reddening, luminosity, and mass functions. Additionally, our findings include the cluster's total mass and the physical characteristics of its most massive stars. Through a statistical analysis and synthetic clusters, we identified Melotte 72's age to be 600+/-60 million years, supplemented by its initial mass function validation. Significantly, our research reveals a prominent gap in the 2-4 solar mass range of stellar mass functions in Melotte 72, indicative of pre-main-sequence spin-down. Moreover, compared to the field, we found an irregularity in the pre-main-sequence distribution of Melotte 72's mass functions. Based on the Gaia DR2 data, the mass of Melotte 72's massive stars in the cluster can be estimated, but their positions remain unclear due to substantial photometric uncertainties. Using the SRaP method which incorporates the BaSeL spectroscopic libraries, we have reconstructed the Melotte 72's cluster spectrum and the cluster's photometric SFRs, displaying a deviated pattern from the conventional full binary initial mass functions. According to our 3D photometry, we found the Melotte 72's cluster radius to be 9.4+/-0.3 degrees and photometric bolometric radius to be 9.8+/-0.3 degrees. Moreover, our research reveals Melotte 72's cluster radius to be slightly thicker in the disk plane at the radius, signifying a dynamic pattern. Using the BaSeL spectroscopic libraries, we found BaFeII 3.8746 mum to be the most prominent feature in the BaFeII spectrum across 3.5-4.0 micrometers. Additionally, we found an inversely BaFeII continuum pattern. Using the PHOENIX models, we have identified Phoenix 19 au 1 mu as the most prominent feature in the BaFeII spectrum across 3.5-4.0 micrometers.

Data analysis applications in medicine, cosmology, and materials science are witnessing growing interest in probabilistic excursion patterns. This research provides the first thorough examination of Betti numbers under the condition of sparse data, using Poisson processes as a mathematical framework. Assuming a smooth manifold, we identify the probability distribution of Betti numbers in homology and cohomology for dimensions one and two, given specific sample size parameters. Numerical evaluations reveal that there's a phase shift in these distributions as the distance between sample points changes. Additionally, local extrema are found in the probability distributions of Betti numbers, and it's confirmed that decreasing distance results in decreasing Betti numbers while their variances and mean values exhibit contrasting behaviors. It's also shown that topological features can provide tighter lower and upper bounds for estimating key parameters of the underlying geometric structure. This study offers relevant practitioners a better understanding of expected topological characteristics of their data sets and how they change with distance, which can be critical for deciding sampling strategies and designing novel algorithms. Moreover, it's verified that persistent homology ignores the underlying geometric structure of data sets more quickly as the distance decreases, due to the response of homology and cohomology dimensions examined in this study. All findings described here were obtained numerically, and there's still a need for analytical solutions that accurately describe probability distributions of Betti numbers, facilitating a deeper understanding of pattern recognition in data. Relevant code used to generate the figures in this research can be found at https://github.com/milicev/pdb. Furthermore, a Python package called Topology-Sampling provides algorithms and recommendations for choosing sample distances that maximize the expected Betti numbers of a data set. Both packages can help designers of algorithms operating on data sets with sparse data achieve greater performance, as demonstrated by the Betti number-based bounds for the homology rank and the eigenvectors of the Gramian matrix. These bounds have also enabled a novel phase shift phenomenon to be identified in the eigenspaces of the Gramian matrix, which could be of independent interest. Relevant code and instructions for executing the provided algorithms can be found at https://github.com/adloos/Topology-sampling. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found that predicting the camera's positioning directly resulted in the best overall performance. When testing the methods with varying levels of noise in the images, our results showed that deep learning-based methods significantly outperformed simpler techniques like widening the baseline or using the cross-validation method. Our found that a noise level of approximately 0.5 pixels was the threshold beyond which the method predicting the camera's positioning directly from images lost accuracy, which is equivalent to about 60 degrees of uncertainty when factored into the camera's rotation. Notably, our results suggested that improving the method's robustness could be achieved by using only smaller images, as they are less susceptible to noise. These findings indicate that leveraging deep learning and using only a single image to calculate the camera's positioning directly may offer better accuracy and reliability compared to traditional methods. Further improvements could be made by training the models on real data to generalize their performance across different applications and domains. A detailed implementation of our work is available at https://github.com/Georgiy.Almenkov/srccamera.

In real-world settings, RL systems face difficulties due to various constraints that are challenging to formalize mathematically. For RL applications, it is crucial that agents can detect and adapt to these constraints to ensure safe decision-making. This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Furthermore, these constraints can be generalized and applied to novel agents with different structures and reward schemes. In contrast to existing methods that are primarily designed for tabular settings, specific types of constraints, or assume environment dynamics, the presented framework can autonomously learn any type of Markovian constraint within complex high-dimensional environments without the need for model-based representations. This capability is successfully demonstrated through constraint inference across various scenarios, such as transferring knowledge from a simulator to a real-world robotic arm and learning constraints for an agent navigating a complex navigation task. Results demonstrate that the inferred constraints can be explicitly enforced, leading to improved performance when compared to compliance-based approaches, and the learned constraints exhibit strong generalizability when applied to alternative agents with different architectures. The code and data for this study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/atchetto/latentconstraints. This work marks a significant advancement in constraint identification for compliant RL systems. Additionally, the proposed framework offers an effective approach for implementing policy compression, allowing for improved portability of agent policies across various environments while ensuring safety, thus paving the way for more reliable agent deployments. Final research findings are presented in a video detailing the results obtained from the different models and benchmark tasks, which can be accessed at https://drive.google.com/drive/u/1/?stsb=1&uig=2&pred=1&from=drive%3E.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, with the ultimate goal of producing a map to an unparalleled degree of accuracy. This article will explore the mission itself, along with the resulting data releases and their potential impact. A detailed overview of the DR1 and DR2 data releases and their initial findings, including DR1 as a precursor to the eagerly anticipated DR2, will also be presented. Furthermore, a review of the DR1 and DR2 findings in terms of their astronomical implications will be examined, with a particular focus on the DR2 data release which significantly surpasses its predecessor. Lastly, an overview of the upcoming data releases will be discussed, with an emphasis on the GDR2 which is expected to greatly enhance our knowledge of astronomical studies. This article is based on a presentation given at the 5th Conference associated with the GAIA mission.

A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions consider the weights fully; some depend on the degree and react sensitively to even small weight changes, a limitation we call "hybrid."
For many scenarios, we advocate using fully-weighted definitions.
We specify requirements for effectively analyzing multiple weighted networks, and propose a new continuous clustering coefficient that meets all the criteria and handles vanishing weights.
We show through synthetic and real-world examples that our continuous clustering coefficient offers better results and its behavior provides valuable insights in situations like noisy networks, heterogeneous systems, and networks derived from inference. It is available as part of the NetworkAnalysis package for Python.

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of training effectiveness and data efficiency. Furthermore, PINNs are shown to outperform purely data-driven neural networks when incorporating additional insights from physics-based models, which can be achieved by optimizing PINNs' loss functions to capture low-dimensional system dynamics. The findings support the development of neural networks that incorporate physical insights to enhance their performance, robustness, and adaptability. Overall, our work aims to understand the effects of data on learning systems with and without physical insight, thereby paving the way for the development of more practical and autonomous learning algorithms for control tasks. The underlying numerical implementation and corresponding experiments are provided in the online repository https://github.com/multidots/learning-from-physbasin. One possible application of this framework involves using PINNs to improve the performance of model predictive control (MPC) methods, as demonstrated in our study using the Koopman operator based low-dimensional model of the double pendulum system. The proposed framework offers a versatile framework that can be used to validate the key tenets of learning by learning, namely data augmentation, model augmentation, and model alignment, across a variety of applications. The implementation of the proposed framework is based on an existing open-source software package, which provides a scalable environment for numerical investigations and computational simulations. One notable aspect of our study involves providing a systematic numerical analysis of the computational requirements and challenges, such as overfitting and data requirements, that might arise during the learning process. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing the orbital Hall effect offers the benefit of eliminating the need for valley-selective light sources, making it more attainable for the valley Hall effect to be implemented in devices.  Further investigation into the differences between the orbital Hall and valley Hall effects in specific mechanisms of light emission is also explored.  Our discovery is initially verified by designing a new gapped graphene structure, where the orbital Hall effect is verified using computational methods.  Our computational models reveal the emergence of a distinct orbital Hall effect even when the valleys remain unreached by the emission sources.  Notably, this phenomenon may present a new method for detecting and manipulating the orbits within gapped graphene, where each orbital state can be selectively targeted with specific emitters.  Our research highlights the value of the orbital Hall effect in achieving the valley Hall effect, showing considerable promise for applications in plasmon-assisted devices, where the convergence of valley and orbital Hall effects may lead to unprecedented control and manipulation of the electron flows based on their indices. A vertex cover of a hypergraph is defined as a set that intersects with every edge of the hypergraph. A vertex cover is considered minimal if none of its subsets result in a hypergraph that possesses property C(k, ρ). This has been proven by observing that a random set of vertices is more likely to have a minimal vertex cover of the smallest size by at least ε, where ε is a positive constant, than to have a set one inch smaller than the smallest size by at least inch less than ε. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. It's a biological implementation of Bayesian inference, where agents utilize their prior knowledge of their world to gather more information through movement and sensing, ultimately reducing uncertainty about their surroundings. Active inference has been successfully translated into a mathematical formula, known as the active Gaussian process, and tested against real-world data from a variety of species, including bees and monkeys. Recent studies have taken this theory to the next level by creating simulated scenarios to study the behavior of unknown agents, while assuming their use of the active inference process. Moreover, the active inference process has been incorporated into a simple robotic system, demonstrating the ease with which it can be employed in a control system, and tested against real-world data from a variety of sensors. Given its impressive performance, the authors believe that active inference offers a powerful framework for understanding and replicating the behavior of living agents and/or designing advanced robotic systems. The provided MATLAB code provides the necessary tools to execute the active inference process, while a accompanying PDF document presents a more in-depth description of the theory along with supporting evidence from recent studies. The related YouTube channel contains video recordings of the active inference process in action, while all data and code can be freely accessed through an open repository on GitHub. Moreover, the paper "Active inference" has been published as a book by Cambridge University Press, while relevant knowledge can also be found through the "ActiveCognition" website. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, the study assesses the capabilities of multiple NLP models with fewer parameters that were fine-tuned on an AES dataset and demonstrates superior results can be achieved by combining these models' outputs, thereby reducing the total number of required parameters. A thorough examination of the study's findings also highlights the importance of long-term dependencies in various model assessments. For the purposes of this research, multiple prevalent NLP models were chosen, including BERT, RoBERTa, BART, and XLNet, with a specific focus on their variants and the addition of a strong, compact language model designed for Computer Oral Exams (COMET) by our research group. Initially, the study investigated the performance of BERT and COMET in three sub-tasks: Essay Evaluation, Grammar Checking (with a focus on error detection), and Machine Translation (a new task for COMET). By evaluating these models' capabilities in Automated Essay Scoring, the study identified areas where human judgment is superior to current NLP technology. Interestingly, the study found that models capable of capturing long-term patterns are essential to performing well in this complex domain. Next, the researchers evaluated a range of models with varying parameter counts (ranging from 84 million to 110 million), highlighting the prevalence of diminishing returns in this case. Finally, the study demonstrated that a specific ensemble of BERT, RoBERTa, BART, XLUNet, and COMET, equipped with a sophisticated fusion mechanism, yields exceptional performance and outperforms current state-of-the-art AES models. By achieving this success with a significantly reduced number of parameters (approximately 20% less), the study provides substantial evidence to dispute the notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. The proposed approach also offers considerable benefits in terms of computational efficiency. To facilitate replication and evaluation, the study's code and AES dataset will be made available under a free open-source license. For the purposes of this research, the name "RoBERTa-Ensemble" has been chosen

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an unsupervised positive box selection process.  In this paper, we present a novel framework, called False Positive Elimination Network (FPEN), to eliminate false positives without supplementary information from the training set.  Compared with existing methods, our framework benefits from two aspects: firstly, the selection of actual boxes is based on the distinct characteristics of positive boxes, rather than relying on the rough bounding box regression like FSAF and MUN, or map alignment like ADA, which often fail to find accurate targets.  Secondly, the unsupervised selection of actual boxes is implemented through an undirected graph optimization algorithm, with energy function designed based on novelty detection, making the selection process easier and more intuitive.  To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conducted unsupervised domain adaptive pedestrian detection experiments on the BDD100K dataset, achieving an impressive mAP from 13.6% to 41.9% with the selection of only 10% positive boxes.  Moreover, the FPEN's performance shows a more robust robustness compared with state-of-the-art methods as evidenced by the results of ablation studies.  Code implementation can be found at https://github.com/ByungjunPark/FalsePositiveEliminationNetwork.  Our work presents a novel insight in addressing the unsupervised domain adaptive object detection challenge.  We hope our findings motivate future research in this area.  Importantly, the proposed framework can also be applied to remove false positives in a semi-supervised setting. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. This study contributes a novel audio enhancement technique for consumer-grade music recordings and conducts an exhaustive analysis of the reliability of conventional audio improvement metrics in the context of music. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our lab-based study involves displaying throwing animations with varying points of release to over 60 participants and using subjective ratings and response times to analyze the data. Furthermore, participants responded faster to late releases in error throws. The findings provide valuable insights for the design of realistic throwing animations in the entertainment and education fields. The study also offers suggestions for the design of interactive applications and outlines potential applications in the entertainment and education sectors. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages a tree-structured DRNN (Doubly-Recurrent Neural Networks) model originally proposed in 2017 by Alvarez-Melis and Jaakola. The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding enhanced by a syntax-aware attention mechanism, differing from prior syntax-based NMT methods that rely on dependency parsing models. Conversely, the presented approach utilizes constituency parsing models, which it posits provides valuable information for translation. Moreover, by incorporating syntactic sentence structure, additional connections are established within the Seq2DRNN+SynC decoder neural network. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed Seq2DRNN architecture yields more natural translations and exhibits superior reordering abilities in comparison to sequential and state-of-the-art syntax-based NMT models. Consequently, it outperforms other models in translation tasks, achieving a 1-2 + 2-3 WMD (Word-level Metrics for Evaluation) score improvement. Notably, the results indicate that incorporating additional syntax information improves translation quality, resulting in a 0.8-1.2 + 1.2-1.6 WMD score improvement, depending on whether the syntax information is incorporated during either encoding or decoding stages. Additional experiments examining various parser types are conducted, and the associated code is available online at the github repository located at https://github.com/yl9559/Seq2DRNN_NMT. Moreover, the results indicate that the proposed approach is compatible with existing sequential NMT models, and the performance gains are more pronounced in cases with heightened syntax diversity. Finally, the results suggest that the majority of the improved performance in the Seq2DRNN+SynC model can be attributed to the syntax information incorporated during decoding. Importantly, the results further indicate that the additional syntax information is beneficial at incorporating both high-level sentence ideass well as fine-grained word-level information.
